exp.0:7:
Here God the Father speaks to his Son and says: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever." The phrase "forever and ever" means for all eternity. The "scepter of righteousness" is a king's scepter, and "righteousness" means justice and uprightness. His kingdom is governed with perfect justice.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 45 to show that Jesus is superior to the angels. The angels are servants and messengers, but the Son is called God and is given an eternal kingdom. In this way the writer encourages Jewish believers to trust in Christ and not to abandon him.

For today: when everything seems unjust or unstable, remember that Jesus reigns, and his government is just and does not end. Entrust your decisions and your worries to him, and seek to live with the same uprightness that he loves.
exp.11:10:
It says that no correction feels joyful while we are receiving it; on the contrary, it hurts and saddens us. But over time it produces a peaceful fruit: a more upright life. Here "chastening" means discipline or training, like that of a father who raises his child. "Exercised" means trained, like an athlete.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians worn down by trials. He compares God to a father who corrects his children out of love. Human parents do this for a short time and with mistakes; God does it for our good and to make us holy. That is why he then asks them to lift their drooping hands and keep going forward.

When you go through a hardship or a correction, do not stay only in the pain. Ask God: "What do you want to teach me?" Trust that he is shaping you, and keep walking with patience.
exp.1:2:
This verse asks a serious question: if we ignore or neglect such a great salvation, how will we escape judgment? Here "salvation" is the word for the rescue God offers, and "neglect" means to give it little importance. This salvation was first announced by the Lord Jesus and then confirmed to the readers by those who heard him directly.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who may have been growing weary or drifting away. He compares the message that came through angels, which was enforced firmly, with the message of the Son, which is even greater. That is why his warning is stronger.

For today: do not take your faith for granted. Set aside time each day to read the Bible and pray, so that you do not slowly drift away from what God has given you.
exp.10:6:
Noah believed what God warned him about something no one could yet see: the flood. Moved by reverence, he built the ark to save his family. The word "prepared" in the verse means he readied or built it. His obedience showed up the unbelief of others, which is what the verse means by saying he condemned the world. God accepted him as righteous because he trusted Him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, encourages Christians to persevere. Earlier he spoke of Enoch, who pleased God through faith. Now he gives Noah as another example, and right after this he will present Abraham, who also obeyed without seeing the whole path.

For today: trust God and obey Him, even when we do not yet see the result. Ask yourself what simple step of obedience God is asking of you, and take it today with reverence and confidence.
exp.2:11:
This verse is a warning to believers. "Take heed" means "be careful, pay attention." The "evil heart of unbelief" is a heart that stops trusting God, and "departing" means drifting away little by little. "The living God" reminds us that God is real and active, not a dead idol.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to abandon their faith. He quotes Psalm 95, which speaks of Israel in the wilderness. That generation saw the works of God, yet they doubted and rebelled, and for that reason they did not enter the rest of the promised land. The author uses that example as a warning.

Today, unbelief almost never arrives all at once; it grows through small doubts and neglect. Seek the encouragement of other believers, as the next verse says, and each day bring your doubts to God in prayer, trusting in his Word.
exp.10:16:
This verse says that Abraham, because he trusted God, was willing to offer Isaac when God tested him. The phrase "was tried" appears in the verse as "was tested" in the source wording, and "only begotten" means only son; Isaac was the child of the promise, although Abraham also had Ishmael. Even so, Abraham acted as one who had already received God's promises.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, encourages believers to remain steadfast. Earlier he spoke of the patriarchs who looked for a heavenly city. Now he shows that Abraham's faith was tested in the hardest way: God had promised him descendants through Isaac, and yet God asked him to give him up. The verses that follow explain that Abraham believed God could raise the dead.

For today: trusting God does not always mean understanding his ways. When something we love seems to be at risk, we can entrust it to him in prayer, remembering that God is faithful to his promises.
exp.5:15:
This verse says that people, when they want to make sure something is true, swear by someone greater than themselves, such as God or a higher authority. Disputes are the arguments or disagreements between people. Giving assurance is what makes an oath a guarantee. In other words, an oath puts an end to arguments because it guarantees that what was said is true.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who needed to stay firm. He has just recalled that God promised Abraham blessing and descendants. He uses the human custom of oaths to explain that God, in swearing, wanted to give even greater assurance to his promise.

For today: when you doubt or feel insecure, remember that God not only promises, but has bound himself to his word in a solemn way. You can rely on that and pray with confidence, waiting patiently as Abraham did.
exp.12:16:
The explanation says that believers should obey their pastors, that is, the leaders of the church, and respect their guidance. The reason is that they watch over the souls of the congregation and will one day have to give account to God. In this way they can do their work with joy and not with grief. Watching means being alert, like a guard. Their watching is done with sorrow and complaint, which is why the verse warns that grief would be of no benefit to you.

The author of Hebrews is unknown; the letter does not give his name. He writes to Christians who needed to persevere. He comes from speaking about praising God and helping others, and moves on to how to live together in community. He asks for prayer for himself, so he also belongs to that circle of leaders and brothers.

For today: pray for your leaders and listen to their teaching with humility, always comparing it with the Bible. Encourage them with a kind word, and support them with your service in the church.
exp.12:12:
It says we should go out to Jesus, outside the camp, and bear the disgrace he endured. The word for camp in this verse refers to the camp itself, and the disgrace is the shame and scorn that come with it. Jesus died outside the city gate, just as the bodies of the animals whose blood was taken into the sanctuary were burned outside the camp.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background who were under pressure and facing rejection. He reminds them of the ritual of the Day of Atonement and asks them not to return to the safety of the old system. Some understand "the camp" as the temple-centered Judaism of that time; others understand it as any religious or social system that rejects Christ.

Today, following Jesus can cost us approval or comfort. When you find yourself misunderstood for living with honesty and faith, remember that he was already there, and go with him with confidence.
exp.11:3:
It says that the readers have not yet reached the point of resisting to the point of shedding their blood, that is, to the point of death, in their struggle against sin. "Not yet" means "not yet." "Striving" speaks of fighting with firmness.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who are tired from pressure and suffering. He has just presented Jesus as an example of endurance to the cross. Now he reminds them with affection that, although their struggle is hard, they have not reached the extreme that Jesus lived. Many think that "sin" here includes the temptation to give up and abandon the faith, but the text does not spell this out.

For today: when you feel worn out from struggling against a temptation or from staying faithful, look to Jesus and remember that he already walked a much harder road. Ask him for strength today and take one more step, without losing heart.
exp.2:14:
This verse repeats an invitation: if you hear God's voice today, do not harden your heart, as happened in the provocation. "While it is said" means "while it is still being said to us." "Provocation" refers to the time when the people of Israel rebelled against God in the wilderness.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, quotes Psalm 95 to encourage Jewish Christians who were tired and tempted to abandon their faith. He reminds them that the generation of Moses heard God, but many of them distrusted him. For this reason he asks them to encourage one another every day.

For today: do not put off your response to God. When you sense that he speaks to you through his Word or through your conscience, obey him that same day, and seek out a brother or sister in the faith who will encourage you to remain steadfast.
exp.9:10:
This verse describes the work of the Jewish priests. Every day they stood in the temple to serve and to offer, again and again, the same animal sacrifices. The word "ministering" means serving in worship. "Taking away sins" means removing them completely, and according to the text, those sacrifices never managed to do that.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, compares the old system with the work of Christ. Earlier he quoted Psalm 40 to show that Jesus came to do God's will. The fact that the sacrifices had to be repeated was a sign that they did not finish the matter. The next verse shows the contrast: Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus has already done what was necessary for our forgiveness. We do not need to try to earn it through repeated efforts or feelings of guilt. We can come near to God with gratitude and confidence, and live in obedience as a response to that love.
exp.11:2:
Consider Jesus with careful attention, the one who endured such great opposition from sinners. The words "think carefully" simply mean "consider" or "look closely." "Opposition" refers to hostility and rejection. The idea of "growing weary" means giving up because of exhaustion. The purpose is that we do not wear ourselves out or give up.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who are tired from pressure and hardship. He has just compared the life of faith to a race and pointed to Jesus, who suffered the cross and now sits with God. Next he reminds them that they have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood for their faith.

When you feel worn out by opposition or trials, spend a few minutes reading how Jesus faced rejection. Ask him for strength to keep going without giving up.
exp.8:0:
This verse says that the first covenant, the one God made with Israel, had rules for worship and an earthly sanctuary. The words "Then verily" simply introduce what follows, meaning "then" or "now." "Ordinances of divine service" are the instructions about how to worship God. "Worldly" here does not mean sinful, but belonging to this present world, made of visible materials.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Christ is better than the old system. Before he speaks of Jesus as high priest, he describes the tabernacle, which was a shadow of something greater.

For today: rituals and sacred places can help us, but they are not the center. Today we can approach God with confidence through Jesus. Ask yourself whether your faith rests on religious customs or on a living relationship with Christ.
exp.4:11:
It says that, given how long they had been believers, they should already be teaching others. Yet they once again needed someone to explain to them the most basic things of God's word. They had come to need the simple teaching of the faith, the kind suited to someone just starting out, and not the solid food meant for the mature. The first lessons, the elementary basics, are what they had gone back to needing.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background. He was speaking about Jesus as high priest according to the order of Melchizedek, but he pauses to correct them lovingly: not because they lacked ability, but because they had become slow to listen and to grow.

For today: do not settle for what you learned at the beginning. Set aside a fixed time each week to study the Bible more deeply, and aim to put what you learn into practice, because that is how a person matures.
exp.12:0:
It says that love between brothers and sisters in the faith must continue, that is, that it must not go out or grow cold. "Brotherly love" is the affection one has for a brother or sister. "Continue" means to remain steady and constant.

Hebrews is a letter whose author we do not know for certain; scholars hold several opinions. It was written to Jewish believers who were facing pressure and hardship. Here, near the end of the letter, the author gives practical advice for living out the faith. This verse opens that section, and what follows shows how that love is lived out: through hospitality, visiting prisoners, and standing with those who suffer.

Today, think of a brother or sister in your church who is going through a hard time. Call them, visit them, or invite them to a meal this week. In this way love does not stay in words, but continues in simple deeds.
exp.7:10:
In the new covenant, it says, no one will have to tell their neighbor or their brother, "Know the Lord," because everyone will know him, from the least to the greatest. "Neighbor" here means the person living nearby or the people close to us. The word "propitious," in the following verse, means merciful.

The writer of Hebrews quotes the promise from Jeremiah 31:31-34. He writes to believers of Jewish background, who were probably tempted to go back to the old ways, in order to show them that Christ brings a better covenant. Here God speaks: he promises a personal knowledge of himself, one that comes from the law written on the heart and from the forgiveness of sins. Scholars debate how this is fully fulfilled, whether it is already happening or something is still to come.

For today: do not be content to know God only through what others tell you. Set aside time to speak with him and to read his Word, and keep encouraging others to grow.
exp.10:13:
This verse says that those who acknowledge they are foreigners and travelers on the earth make it clear that they are looking for a home of their own, a homeland.

The author of Hebrews is speaking of Abraham, Sara, and other believers of the Old Testament. They died trusting in God's promises, although they did not see them fulfilled. By calling themselves strangers and sojourners on the earth, they showed that their hearts were set on something better than what they had left behind: the heavenly homeland. The author wants to encourage his readers to persevere in faith.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we live as those who have placed their hope in God. This does not mean neglecting this life, but not clinging to money, success, or comfort as if they were the final goal. We can live with generosity and patience, remembering that what is best comes from God.
exp.12:10:
This verse recalls what happened on the Day of Atonement. The high priest carried the blood of certain animals into the Most Holy Place to ask for forgiveness of sin. But the bodies of those animals were not eaten: they were burned outside the camp of Israel.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to return to their former customs. He uses this image to prepare what follows: Jesus, the final sacrifice, also suffered outside the city gate.

For today: following Christ sometimes means standing outside what others accept or approve. Ask Him for courage to be faithful to Him, even when it costs you rejection, knowing that He has already gone through that and walks with you.
exp.6:7:
This verse compares two groups who receive tithes. On one side are the Levitical priests, who are mortal men: they collect the tithe, but then they die and others take their place. On the other side is Melchizedek, of whom Scripture bears witness that he lives, meaning that his death is not mentioned.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers of Jewish background, who were probably tempted to return to the old ways. He wants to show that Christ, a priest after the order of Melchizedek, is superior to the Levitical priesthood. Scholars debate whether Melchizedek literally lives or whether the point is only the silence of the account about his death (Genesis 14; Psalm 110:4).

For today: our hope does not depend on leaders who die and are replaced, but on Jesus, who lives forever. You can pray today with confidence, knowing that he intercedes for you.
exp.5:16:
This verse says that God wanted to make completely clear to the heirs of the promise that his plans do not change. So, in addition to promising, he made an oath. "Counsel" means his purpose or decision, and "immutability" means that it does not change.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who are weary and tempted to give up. He has just spoken of Abraham, who waited patiently and received the promise. Just as people swear an oath to settle a matter, God also swore. He did not do this because his word was weak, but to give us greater assurance. The "heirs" are those who trust God as Abraham did.

When you doubt or when the waiting grows long, remember that God not only promised but also bound himself with an oath. You can rest your hope on his faithful character, and pray with confidence, even when you do not see quick answers.
exp.10:9:
This verse says that Abraham was waiting for a city with firm foundations, meaning one that is stable and lasting. Its designer and its builder is God himself. While Abraham lived in tents, he looked toward something more secure than any house in this world.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, encourages tired believers to keep trusting God. To do this, he goes through examples of faith from the Old Testament. Abraham obeyed without knowing his destination and lived as a stranger in the promised land. Many understand that this "city" points to the hope of heaven, although there is debate about how to describe it precisely.

For today: when your plans feel unstable or uncertain, remember that your final security is in God. Live with patience, generosity, and obedience, without clinging too tightly to what is passing.
exp.7:2:
Every high priest, the verse says, is appointed to present gifts and sacrifices to God. Gifts here means offerings or presents. So if Jesus is our High Priest, he also had to have something to offer.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, wrote to Christians of Jewish background who knew the system of sacrifices well. He explains that Jesus serves in the heavenly sanctuary, not in the earthly temple. Later in the letter, it makes clear that what Christ offered was his own life.

For today: you do not have to draw near to God on the strength of your own merits or try to make up for your failures. Jesus has already offered what was needed. You can pray with confidence and gratitude, knowing that you have a High Priest who represents you before God.
exp.9:24:
This verse calls us not to stop meeting together as believers, as some have made a habit of doing. Instead, we should encourage one another, and all the more as we see the day drawing near.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians under pressure and tempted to abandon their faith. The verses before this one call them to hold firm and to stir one another up to love and good works. The day is usually understood as the return of Christ and the final judgment, though some also connect it with events close to the author's own time.

For today: find a community of faith and take part in it faithfully. Don't go only to receive, but also to encourage someone with a word, a prayer, or a visit this week.
exp.4:0:
This verse says that every high priest is chosen from among human beings themselves. His work is to represent the people before God and to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. The word "high priest" here means the chief priest, and the "gifts" are offerings or gifts brought to God.

The author of Hebrews is unknown; tradition has proposed several names, but there is no certainty. He writes to believers with a Jewish background, and he begins to explain how Jesus is the perfect priest. To do this, he first describes what a high priest did in Israel, and then he will show how Christ fulfills and surpasses that role.

For today: God wanted our mediator to be someone who understands human weakness. When you feel far from God or ashamed of your failures, remember that you can draw near to Him with confidence, because Jesus knows what we live through and intercedes for you.
exp.3:12:
This verse says that nothing created can hide from God. Everything is laid bare and open before his eyes, that is, completely uncovered, with nothing to cover it. It also says that we will have to give an account to him, that is, answer for our lives. The phrase "every creature" means any creature at all. The word "manifest" means visible, plain to see.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to give up. Using the example of the people in the wilderness, he warns them not to harden their hearts. God's word reveals the deepest part of us, and this God who sees everything is also the one who receives us through Jesus, our great High Priest.

Today we can stop pretending before God. Since he already knows everything, we can pray with sincerity, confess our failings, and draw near with confidence, because Jesus understands us.
exp.2:8:
It says that the ancestors of Israel tested God in the desert. Here, the word "tested" means putting God's patience to the test by doubting Him, and the word "proved" carries the same sense. Even so, for forty years they saw the works of God: the manna, the water from the rock, His daily care. "Your fathers" are the Israelites who came out of Egypt.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 and says that the Holy Spirit is the one speaking. He writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to abandon their faith in Christ. He reminds them that seeing God's works is not enough if the heart becomes hard. God is the one speaking in the quotation, and that is why the text goes on to speak of His anger and His oath.

Today: do not get so used to God's blessings that you begin to doubt Him. When a difficulty comes, remember what He has already done for you and trust Him, with a heart ready to obey Him today.
exp.12:19:
This verse begins a prayer of blessing. It says that God is "the God of peace," the one who brought Jesus back from the dead, and it calls Jesus "that great shepherd of the sheep." This happened "through the blood of the everlasting covenant," that is, through the blood of the covenant or agreement that never ends.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, closes his letter with a prayer for his readers. Earlier he asked them to pray for him. Throughout the letter he has explained that Jesus established a new and better covenant. Here he sums up that teaching and asks that God strengthen them.

For today: when you feel tired or lost, remember that your shepherd lives and cares for you. You can pray with confidence, asking God to help you do his will, because he himself gives the strength to do it.
exp.5:19:
He says that Jesus entered for us as the one who goes ahead, into the place where our hope reaches: the presence of God. The one who goes ahead opens the way so that others can follow. A high priest is the one who presents the people before God. "For ever" means forever. His priesthood is of a different kind from Aaron's, not based on family inheritance and not ended by death.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers who were at risk of losing heart. He has just spoken of hope as an anchor of the soul, and now he shows where that anchor is fastened: in Jesus, who has already entered the heavenly sanctuary. Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14 and in Psalm 110.

For today: when you feel shaken by uncertainty, remember that your hope does not depend on your own strength. Jesus has already reached where you are going, and he prays for you. Rest in him and speak with God with confidence.
exp.11:4:
They say the readers have forgotten a word of encouragement that God speaks to them as to children. That word, taken from Proverbs 3:11-12, says: do not despise the Lord's correction, and do not give up when he rebukes you. Here "correction" means discipline or training, not only a punishment for a fault. "Give up" means to surrender.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers worn down by opposition and trials. He asked them to look to Jesus, who endured hostility. Now he reminds them that suffering does not mean God has abandoned them. On the contrary, the following text explains that the Father corrects those he loves as children.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, do not rush to think that God has rejected you. Pray sincerely and ask him what he wants to teach you, without giving up or hardening your heart. His fatherly care is still with you.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that a rest still remains prepared for those who belong to God. The word "rest" means peace, relief, and calm. The idea of "remaineth" means it is still pending and available; it has not run out.

The writer of Hebrews is speaking to believers who were tempted to give up. He reminds them that Israel did not enter that rest because of their disobedience, and that even Joshua, when he led them into the promised land, did not fully fulfill that promise. That is why David spoke of another "today." Christians understand this rest as resting in God and trusting in his work, with a fullness that will be completed in the future. There are different ways of explaining it.

Today you can stop living to earn God's favor through your own effort. Pause, trust in him, and hand him your burdens with faith and obedience.
exp.0:13:
This verse says that the angels are spirits who serve God. He sends them to help those who will receive salvation as their inheritance. The word "ministering" here means serving or helping. Salvation in this verse refers to being saved, not just to physical health. And those who will receive what God promised are the heirs.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, compares Jesus with the angels. The angels are admirable, but they are servants. Jesus, by contrast, is the Son, and God invited him to sit at his right hand. In this way the author shows that Christ is superior and worthy of complete trust.

For today: you can rest knowing that God cares for you in ways you do not see. You do not need to worship angels or seek them out; your trust should be in Jesus. Today, thank God for his care and serve others with humility, as the angels do.
exp.9:19:
He says that Jesus opened for us a new and living way toward God. "Consecrated" means that he inaugurated it, or put it into use for the first time. That way passes through the veil, which is the curtain of the temple that separated the Most Holy Place, and the text explains that this veil is his flesh, that is, his body given up on the cross.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to give up. He reminds them that Christ's sacrifice is sufficient and that no further offerings for sin are needed. For this reason he encourages them to draw near to God with confidence. There are different views on how exactly to understand the image of the veil, but the central idea is clear: Christ opened the way of access.

For today: when you feel far from God or unworthy, do not wait to make yourself presentable first. Pray with confidence, because Jesus has already opened the door.
exp.5:10:
It says that the author wants each believer to keep showing the same earnest effort, the same eagerness, that they have already shown, and to keep doing so to the very end. The goal is that hope be fully fulfilled, that is, that it become complete certainty.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, has just issued a stern warning about the danger of drifting away. Now he speaks with tenderness, calling them dear friends. He acknowledges their service to the saints and tells them that God does not forget that love. He asks them not to slacken, because faith is tested over time.

For today: do not lose heart if your service seems to bear no fruit. Choose one concrete act of love, such as visiting, helping, or praying for someone, and keep it up faithfully, trusting that God sees and does not forget your work.
exp.12:8:
It says we should not be carried back and forth by varied and strange teachings. It is good for the heart to be strengthened by God's grace, and not by food rules, that is, rules about what we eat. Those rules never truly helped the people who depended on them.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He has just reminded them that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. For that reason they should not change direction because of new teachings. He probably has in mind ritual rules about food and sacrifices, though some think he means other practices.

For today: when a teaching appears that adds requirements for earning God's favor, compare it with Christ and his grace. Keep resting your heart on what Jesus has already done, not on what you manage to accomplish.
exp.9:16:
This verse says that God promises to remember our sins and our wrongdoings no more. The word "iniquities" means acts of wickedness or injustice. The word "adds" continues the quotation from Jeremiah 31 that comes from the previous verse. "Will remember no more" does not mean that God forgets, but that He no longer holds them against us.

The author of Hebrews explains that the Holy Spirit spoke in the Scripture about the new covenant. He writes to believers of Jewish background, and he wants to show that Christ's sacrifice is sufficient. That is why, in the following verse, he says that no other offering for sin is needed any longer.

For today: if you have trusted in Christ, do not carry guilt for sins that have already been forgiven. When you remember a past mistake, bring it to God with gratitude, learn from it, and live in freedom and confidence.
exp.5:0:
Leaving behind the basic teachings about Christ, the believer is urged to move on toward maturity ("perfection" here means growing, becoming complete). The foundation does not need to be laid again: repenting of dead works (actions that do not give life before God) and believing in God.

The author of Hebrews is unknown; the letter is addressed to believers with a Jewish background who were tempted to turn back. He rebuked them for still acting like children in the faith (5:12-14). That is why he calls them to mature. Some think this list of basic teachings reflects practices known in Judaism, but this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: foundations are important, but a house does not stay only at the foundation. Make time a steady habit of reading the Bible, praying, and serving, so that your faith keeps growing and does not stall.
exp.9:0:
The explanation says that the law of Moses was like a shadow: it showed from a distance the good things God would bring, but it was not the reality itself. For this reason, the sacrifices that were repeated every year could never make those who came to worship complete, fully cleansed before God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to return to the old customs. He explains to them that Christ fulfills what the law only announced. Here he begins to show that a sacrifice repeated again and again points to the need for one better and final.

For today: do not trust in religious routines or in your efforts to feel clean before God. Rest in what Christ has already done, and let that assurance lead you to draw near to Him with confidence and gratitude.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that God was displeased with that generation of Israel. Being angry with them means that he was indignant and grew angry with them. Their hearts went astray, wandering from one place to another without direction. And although they saw God's works, they did not come to know his ways, that is, they did not learn to live as he teaches.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 and presents God speaking about the people who came out of Egypt. For forty years in the desert they doubted and complained, even while witnessing miracles. The writer uses this to warn believers: do not repeat that same unbelief.

For today: it is not enough to see or hear what God does; we must respond to him with trust and obedience. When you feel your heart drifting or hardening, stop, pray, and ask God to teach you his ways.
exp.8:17:
This verse says that even the first covenant, the one God made with Israel through Moses, did not begin without blood.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He has been explaining that a will requires the death of the one who made it. With this he prepares the way to show that Christ, by his blood, inaugurated a new and better covenant. The verses that follow recall when Moses sprinkled blood on the book and on the people.

For today: our forgiveness does not depend on our efforts, but on Christ's giving of himself. You can draw near to God with gratitude and confidence, without trying to earn what has already been paid for at such great cost.
exp.9:23:
It says we should pay close attention to one another, that is, think about the good of others and not only about ourselves. The purpose is "to stir up" one another, an old-fashioned phrase that here does not mean to annoy, but to encourage or spur on, so that we grow in love and in good works.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background who were facing pressure and weariness. After explaining that Christ is our high priest and opens the way to God for us, he invites them to draw near with faith, to hold firmly to hope, and to care for one another. The next verse urges them not to give up meeting together.

For today: think of someone in your church or close circle and encourage them this week with a message, a visit, or a concrete help. In this way love becomes action.
exp.9:5:
It says that God took no delight in the burnt offerings (offerings completely burned on the altar) or in the sin offerings (sacrifices meant to cover guilt).

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 40 and presents these words as spoken by Christ when he came into the world. He explains that the blood of animals could not truly take away sins. Those sacrifices, which the law required, pointed to something greater. God prepared a body for Christ, who came to do the Father's will and to offer himself.

For today: let us not trust in rituals or religious efforts to feel clean before God. Let us rest in what Christ has done for us and respond with sincere obedience that springs from a thankful heart.
exp.6:5:
This verse speaks of Melchizedek. It says that he did not belong to the family of Levi, that is, he did not have Israel's priestly descent. Even so, he received tithes (a tenth part) from Abraham and blessed him, even though Abraham was the one who had received God's promises.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers with a Jewish background, and he wants to show that Christ is superior to the Levitical priesthood. He recalls the meeting in Genesis 14: Abraham gave tithes to Melchizedek and was blessed by him. The argument is that the priesthood of Melchizedek, to which Christ is compared, is of a higher order than that of Levi.

For today: we do not need human go-betweens to come to God, because Christ is our priest. We can approach Him with confidence, and respond to Him with gratitude, honoring Him with what we have and with our lives.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that Jesus, who makes us holy (sets us apart and cleanses us for God), and we, who are made holy, come from one and the same origin: God the Father. For this reason Jesus is not ashamed to call us brothers. The word "but" in the verse above is what the old text renders as "empero," and the word translated "salvation" in the verse before it is what the old text calls "salud."

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who needed encouragement. He has just explained that Jesus became human and suffered in order to bring many children to glory. For this reason he can identify with us. The verses that follow quote the Psalms and Isaiah to show that family bond.

For today: even when you sometimes feel unworthy or full of faults, Christ is not ashamed of you. Come to him with confidence, as to a brother who understands you, and treat other believers with affection too, because they are your family.
exp.7:0:
What the verse says, in short, is that the most important point of everything explained so far is this: we have a high priest who has already sat down at the right hand of God's throne, here called the Majesty, in the heavens. The word "sum" means summary or main point. "Right hand" is the place of honor and authority.

Hebrews is a letter of unknown authorship; several names have been proposed, but none is certain. It was written to believers with a Jewish background who were tempted to return to their former practices. The author shows them that Jesus is better than the priests of the temple, because he serves in heaven, in the true sanctuary.

For today: if Jesus is seated beside God, your prayer does not go unattended. You can approach God with confidence, without fear, knowing that someone with authority and compassion intercedes for you.
exp.8:5:
This verse says that, with everything of the tabernacle already set in its place, the priests went in continually into the first part, called the Holy Place, to carry out their service of worship. The "service of God" is the daily religious duties, such as offering incense and tending the lamps and the bread.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He describes the tabernacle to show that this system had limits. The priests entered one part, but only the high priest, once a year, entered the most holy place. All of this pointed to Christ opening a better way.

Today we can draw near to God without human go-betweens or repeated rituals, because Jesus has already opened the way. Pray with confidence and gratitude, knowing that God receives you because of what Christ has done.
exp.10:15:
They did not long for the country they had left, the author says, but desired something better: a heavenly homeland. For this reason God is not ashamed to be called their God. God had a city ready for them.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who were weary and tempted to turn back. He speaks of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who lived as strangers in Canaan, trusting in promises they did not see fulfilled during their lifetimes. We do not know for certain who wrote the letter, but its message is clear: faith looks forward, not back.

For today: when you feel tempted to return to what God has already brought you out of, remember that He is preparing something better for you. Live with hope and with open hands, not clinging too tightly to what passes away, because your God is not ashamed of you.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that Jesus came to free the people who spent their whole lives held captive by the fear of dying. That fear kept them as if they were slaves.

Context: the author of Hebrews does not name himself, and we cannot be certain who he was. He writes to show that Jesus truly became human, sharing in flesh and blood. By dying, he defeated the devil, who held power over death. In this way, Jesus identified himself with us in order to rescue us.

For today: if the fear of death or of the future weighs on you, you can bring it to Jesus in prayer. He knows human suffering and has already overcome death. Remembering his resurrection can bring you peace, so that you live with more freedom and confidence, and not with anguish.
exp.6:1:
Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth part of everything he had recovered. The text explains the meaning of his name: "King of righteousness." He was also king of Salem, which means "King of peace."

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is a priest greater than the priests of the temple. To do this, he uses Melchizedek, who appears briefly in Genesis 14. The meanings of his name and of his city point to what Christ brings.

For today: Jesus unites righteousness and peace. If you have failed and feel restless, come to Him with confidence. And seek to live justly and peacefully with those around you.
exp.8:14:
He says that Jesus is the mediator of a new covenant (the older text says "testament"). His death took place to forgive the transgressions committed against God under the first covenant. Thus, those called by God receive what was promised: an eternal inheritance.

The book of Hebrews was written to believers with a Jewish background; no one knows for certain who its author was. It had been comparing the sacrifices in the temple with the sacrifice of Christ. The animals cleansed the outward person, but Christ cleanses the conscience. The Greek word can mean "covenant" or "testament," and the following verses play on both meanings.

If you feel guilty for past failures, remember that Christ has already paid with his death. You can come before God with confidence, not to earn his favor, but to serve him with gratitude.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that the first covenant, the one God made with Israel through Moses, had a fault. If it had been faultless, there would have been no need to look for another. "Faultless" means without defect, and the second part of the verse means that a second covenant would not have been sought.

The author of Hebrews wrote to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to return to the old law. He shows them that Christ is the mediator of a better covenant. He then quotes the prophet Jeremiah, who had already announced a new covenant. The fault lay in the people's failure to remain faithful, not in any failure on God's part.

For today: do not trust your own efforts to be perfect before God. Rest in Christ, who gives you a new heart and complete forgiveness. Obey God out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.4:2:
The explanation says that the human high priest, being full of weakness, had to present offerings for his own sins just as he did for the sins of the people.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows with certainty who he was) explains how the priesthood of Israel worked. He wants his readers to understand that the priest was someone like them, who could sympathize with the weak. This prepares the contrast with Christ, whom he presents shortly afterward as the High Priest called by God.

For today: recognizing our own weakness makes us more humble and compassionate toward others. If we have been called to guide or correct someone, let us do so remembering that we too need the forgiveness and grace of God.
exp.11:7:
This verse says that if a person has never received correction from God, something is wrong, because all of his children receive it. Here "chastisement" means discipline or fatherly instruction, not simple punishment meant to make someone suffer. "Bastards" refers to children who are not legitimate, who are not recognized as part of the family.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were going through trials and felt discouraged. He reminds them that discipline is not a sign of abandonment, but that God treats them as beloved children, just as a good father corrects his children.

Today, when God corrects you or you face a difficulty, do not immediately think that he has rejected you. Ask him what he wants to teach you, and receive that correction with humility, trusting that it comes from a Father who loves you.
exp.9:6:
It says that someone presents himself to God with complete readiness: "Here I am, ready to do your will." The phrase "at the head of the book" refers to the beginning of a scroll, that is, to what the Scriptures already said about him. "Behold, I come" means "here I am."

The author of Hebrews puts these words in the mouth of Christ as he comes into the world. He quotes Psalm 40:6-8 to show that animal sacrifices were not the final purpose; God wanted obedience from the heart. Christ offers himself, and so the new replaces the old. Some understand "the book" to mean the whole Old Testament; others, a particular passage.

For today: Jesus shows us that what God seeks is a willing heart. Today you can simply say to him, "Here I am, Lord," and obey him in something concrete this day.
exp.6:21:
This verse says that Jesus is the guarantor of a better covenant. A guarantor is someone who takes responsibility and ensures that a promise will be kept. In this verse, "testament" means "covenant," that is, the agreement God makes with his people. So Jesus is the sure guarantee of a covenant superior to the previous one.

The writer is the author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know with certainty. He speaks to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to return to the old ways. He has just shown that God swore that Jesus would be a priest forever, something that was not said of the Levitical priests. That oath of God is the basis of the guarantee: the covenant rests on a firm promise.

For today: when you doubt whether God will sustain you, remember that your relationship with him does not depend on your steadiness, but on Jesus, who lives forever and stands surety for you. Rest in him and pray with confidence.
exp.8:16:
Here "testament" is understood as a document of inheritance. The "testator" is the person who leaves that inheritance. The verse says that a testament has force only when the person has died. While they are alive, what they promised cannot be claimed.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that the death of Christ was necessary so that those who are called might receive the eternal inheritance. The Greek word can be translated "covenant" or "testament," and scholars debate whether the author plays on both meanings.

Today you can receive forgiveness and eternal life as a gift, not as a wage. Rest in what Christ has already done, and let that lead you to thank him every day.
exp.7:5:
It says that Jesus now has a ministry far more excellent than that of the ancient priests. The reason is that he is the mediator, that is, the one who brings God and people together, of a better covenant. A covenant is a solemn commitment of God to his people. This new covenant rests on better promises.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers of Jewish background, perhaps tempted to return to the old customs. He has just said that the priests of the temple served as a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. Now he shows that Christ is the reality. Soon he will quote Jeremiah's promise about a new covenant.

For today: you do not have to approach God in fear or trying to earn his favor. Jesus is your mediator, and God's promises rest on him. Today you can pray with confidence, knowing that he presents you before the Father.
exp.9:9:
This verse says that God makes us holy, meaning he sets us apart for himself and cleanses us, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ. He did it once for all, without any need to repeat it. "By the which will" refers to God's plan that Jesus came to carry out.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He quotes Psalm 40 as the words of Christ: "Here I am, to do your will." He wants to show that the animal sacrifices, repeated every day, could not take away sins, but Jesus' sacrifice could.

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through effort or carry guilt that has already been forgiven. When you fail, return to God with confidence, remembering that Christ's work is already complete, and live grateful, obeying him with joy.
exp.6:14:
This verse says that what the author has been explaining becomes even more clear: that God has appointed another priest, "after the similitude of Melchisedec." The word "evident" means plain and very clear. The phrase about "there ariseth" means that he appears, or is appointed by God. It refers to Jesus.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to believers from a Jewish background. He shows them that Jesus is a priest, even though he was from the tribe of Judah and not from Levi, which was the priestly tribe. For that reason a different pattern was needed: Melchisedec, a priest who came before the law of Moses.

For today: you do not need intermediaries or personal merits to draw near to God. Jesus is your priest forever. Today you can pray with confidence, knowing that he represents you before the Father.
exp.8:2:
This verse describes the second part of the tabernacle, the place that was behind a curtain. The curtain that separated the spaces is the veil, and the sacred area behind it, where the ark of the covenant stood, was the Holiest of all. Here the word "tabernacle" refers to that second section of the tent of worship.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers of Jewish background. He reminds them how worship was carried out under the first covenant, so that he can later show that Christ brings something better. First he describes in detail the place where God made His presence known.

Today we can be thankful that Jesus opened the way to God. What once lay behind a veil, we can now approach in prayer with confidence, without depending on rituals or human mediators.
exp.11:5:
This verse says that the Lord corrects those he loves. The word "chastens" here means to discipline or train, as a father does with his children. "Scourges" is a strong image for firm correction. "Every son whom he receives" means everyone whom God accepts as his own.

The author of Hebrews writes to Christians who were weary from hardships. He quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 to remind them that suffering does not mean God has abandoned them. On the contrary, many understand that God uses trials to shape them as a good father would. Interpreters debate which specific trials he had in mind, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you go through correction or difficulty, do not lose heart right away. Ask God what he wants to teach you, and trust that his dealings come from love, not rejection.
exp.10:30:
This verse says that Rahab, the woman who had been a prostitute, did not perish along with those who did not believe in God. This happened because she had faith and welcomed the spies in peace, that is, she received them kindly and protected them. The unbelievers are those who refused to believe in God and to obey Him. The spies are the men Joshua sent to scout out Jericho.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, gives examples of people who trusted in God and acted accordingly. He has just spoken of the fall of the walls of Jericho. Rahab appears in Joshua 2 and 6: she had heard what God had done for Israel and recognized His power. It is striking that a foreign woman with a marked past is mentioned.

For today: true faith shows itself in concrete actions. No one is outside God's care because of their past. Today you can trust in Him and take a step of obedience, even if it costs you.
exp.1:5:
Hebrews 2:6 says that someone, in a certain place in Scripture, bore witness with a question: what is a human being, that God should remember him, and what is the son of man, that God should come to visit him? "Yet" means "but," and "visit" here means to look after or care for.

The writer of Hebrews does not say who the speaker is, but he quotes Psalm 8, written by David. He wants to show that the world to come will not be placed under the angels, but under human beings, and finally under Jesus, who became a man. Many understand that the phrase "son of man" points to Christ, although it also speaks of humanity in general.

For today: even when you sometimes feel small or overlooked, God remembers you and cares for you. Rest in that, and live with gratitude and dignity.
exp.9:25:
It says that if someone sins on purpose, after having come to know the truth of the gospel, no other sacrifice remains that can save them. "Sinning deliberately" speaks of sinning in a conscious and persistent way; "no sacrifice remains" means that outside of Christ there is no other offering that forgives.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were tempted to abandon Christ and return to their former practices. He has just encouraged them to meet together and to encourage one another. Then he warns them seriously: rejecting Christ knowingly leaves a person without hope, because his sacrifice is the only one. Christians interpret this warning in different ways: some see a total falling away, others a warning to examine one's faith.

Today, take sin seriously, but do not turn away from the church. Stay close to other believers, confess your failings, and come to Christ with humility.
exp.11:17:
This verse says that believers have not come to the mount that could be touched, that is, to a real, physical mountain. It speaks of fire that burned, of a whirlwind or strong wind, of darkness and of tempest. All of that describes how Israel came to Mount Sinai.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background who were under pressure. He compares Sinai, where the law was given amid fear and distance, with the grace of Christ, which is described in the verses that follow. Earlier he had warned against despising what they had received, as Esau did.

Today, we can draw near to God without paralyzing fear, because Christ opened the way. That is not carelessness: it is humble confidence. Today you can pray with sincerity, remembering that God receives you by grace.
exp.10:22:
The explanation says that Moses' parents hid him during his first three months of life. They did so because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were not afraid of the command of the king of Egypt. Some older words appear here: the word for "was" is written in an old form that is just "was", and "gave" is simply "gave". The word for "command" here means an order or decree.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, is recalling people of faith from the Old Testament to encourage his readers to keep trusting God. According to Exodus 1 and 2, the pharaoh had ordered that the Hebrew baby boys be killed. The text credits the action to the parents' faith, not simply to human cleverness. Some think the word for "beautiful" suggests that they saw God's hand in him, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: faith is sometimes seen in simple, brave decisions, such as protecting someone vulnerable even when it is frightening. Trust God and do the right thing within your reach, even when you cannot see the whole future.
exp.10:20:
He says that Jacob, near death, blessed the two sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, and worshipped God leaning upon the top of his staff. The staff is a walking stick, and "leaning upon" simply means resting his weight on it.

The phrase about the staff comes from an ancient Greek translation of Genesis 47:31; the Hebrew text can be read as "the head of the bed," and for that reason it is explained in more than one way.

The writer of Hebrews is giving examples of people who trusted God's promises even though they did not see them fulfilled. Jacob, weak and old, looked ahead and believed that God would keep his word with his descendants.

For today: faith does not fade with old age or weakness. Even at the end of life we can worship God and bless others, leaving them words of hope and trust in Him.
exp.6:18:
The explanation says that the law of Moses could not bring anyone to perfection, that is, to a full and complete relationship with God. But now a better hope is introduced, and through it we are able to draw near to God. The explanation also notes a point about the wording of the verse: the phrase that means "drew near" in the verse above is the same idea as drawing near to God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not given in the text, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that Jesus is a priest forever, in the manner of Melchizedek, and not according to the Levitical priesthood. For this reason the old commandment about the priesthood is set aside: it was weak and unable to give full access to God. That better hope is Christ himself.

Today you can draw near to God without depending on your merits or your performance. When you feel that you do not measure up, pray with confidence, remembering that Jesus, your priest, has already opened the way to God.
exp.2:13:
We are said to be "partakers of Christ," that is, we share in his life and his blessings, on the condition that we remain firm to the end in the confidence we had at the beginning. Here "hold fast" means to keep hold of and maintain, and "confidence" means assurance and faith in God.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to Jewish Christians who were tempted to give up. He reminds them of the people of Israel, who left Egypt but hardened their hearts in the wilderness through unbelief. He warns that true faith shows itself by persevering. Some Christians read this as a warning that salvation can be lost; others read it as proof that genuine faith endures. Both agree on the need to persevere.

Today you can encourage someone in your church or family with a word of comfort, and you can also let yourself be encouraged. In this way faith stays alive in difficult days.
exp.11:20:
This verse says that what happened at Mount Sinai was so frightening that even Moses, the leader of the people, was filled with fear. "Terrible" here means causing deep dread, not simply something bad. Being "filled with fear" means being overcome with dread, and "quaking" speaks of a real trembling of the body.

The author of Hebrews compares two mountains. He recalls how Israel received the law amid trumpets, voices, and limits that no one could cross. This statement from Moses does not appear word for word in Exodus; it is thought that the author is recalling or summarizing a tradition, and scholars explain this in different ways. His purpose is to show that, before God, the people felt distant and afraid, so that he can then contrast this with the access we now have in Christ.

Today we can draw near to God with confidence through Jesus, without forgetting that he remains holy. Cultivate a sincere reverence when you pray and worship.
exp.9:11:
He says that Jesus, after offering himself once and for all as a sacrifice for sins, sat down at the right hand of God. The words "at the right hand" are an older way of saying "on the right side," a place of honor and authority. "For ever" means that this sacrifice holds for all time and never needs to be repeated.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers with a Jewish background, and we do not know for certain who he was. He compares the priests of the temple, who offered sacrifices every day without ever finishing the task, with Jesus, who completed the work. That is why he sits down: his work of forgiveness is finished.

Today you can rest in the fact that your forgiveness does not depend on your efforts or on repeating rituals to earn God's favor. When guilt accuses you, remember that Christ has already done what was necessary. Come near to God with gratitude and confidence, not with fear.
exp.2:7:
This verse asks us not to close our hearts to God. "Harden" means becoming stubborn and unwilling to listen. "Provocation" is the rebellion that angers someone, and "temptation" here means they put God to the test, doubting him. The "wilderness" recalls the time when Israel walked toward the promised land.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 and says that it is the Holy Spirit who speaks. He writes to believers who could grow weary and turn back. He reminds them that the people of Israel, even after seeing the works of God, rebelled in the wilderness. It is a warning not to repeat that story and to stay firm in Christ.

For today: when you sense that God is speaking to you through his Word, do not put it off for later. Respond with humility and obedience today, even if you are tired or doubting. A soft heart allows itself to be guided.
exp.12:13:
This verse says that in this world we do not have a city that lasts forever. For that reason, believers seek the future city that God is preparing.

The author of Hebrews wrote to believers who were suffering rejection for following Jesus. He says that Jesus suffered outside the gate, that is, outside Jerusalem, and he invites us to go out to him outside the camp, bearing his disgrace. The identity of the writer of the book is not known with certainty. Afterward, the text speaks of praising God and helping others.

Today we can live with open hands: not clinging to material things or to the applause of others. With that hope, let us use our time and resources to praise God and do good to those around us.
exp.11:25:
This verse says that God's voice, when he spoke at Mount Sinai, made the earth shake. But now God has promised something greater: "Yet once more," that is, "once more," he will shake not only the earth but also heaven.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who faced pressure and temptation to abandon the faith. He quotes the prophet Haggai (2:6) and recalls Sinai to warn them: if it was serious to reject God when he spoke on the earth, it is more serious to reject him when he speaks from heaven through Jesus.

For today: when everything around you seems unstable, rely on what does not move, the kingdom of God. Listen carefully to his voice and respond to him with confidence and reverence.
exp.9:22:
This verse invites us to hold firmly to what we confess to believe, without doubting or wavering. "Profession" here means a public declaration of faith, and "wavering" means to hesitate, like a wave that rises and falls. The reason is simple: God is faithful, and he keeps what he promised.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were tired and tempted to give up. He has just explained that Jesus is the great priest who opens the way to God for us. For that reason he now encourages them to draw near with confidence, not to let go of their hope, and to stay united.

For today: when you doubt or feel weary, remember a specific promise of God and repeat it in prayer. Also, look for other believers who can encourage you, because faith is better sustained in company.
exp.7:11:
God promises that he will be merciful toward the wrongdoing of his people. "Merciful" means compassionate and ready to forgive. He says that as for their sins and their iniquities, he will remember them no more, that is, he will not hold them against them to punish them, nor will he use them against them.

The author of Hebrews quotes the prophecy of Jeremiah 31 about the new covenant. He writes to believers of Jewish background to show them that Christ brings something better than the old covenant. This verse is the foundation for the promises before it: God writes his law on the heart, and everyone knows him, because forgiveness comes first. That God will "remember them no more" does not mean he forgets, but that he decides not to carry that sin against us any longer.

Today, if you have trusted in Christ, do not live bound by guilt that has already been forgiven. Come before God with confidence, confess whatever weighs on you, and rest in his forgiveness.
exp.11:15:
This verse warns that no one among you should be sexually immoral or profane, like Esau. A fornicator is someone who lives in sexual immorality. A profane person is someone who treats what is sacred as having no value. Esau traded something very valuable for a bowl of food.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to Christians who were weary and tempted to abandon their faith. He asks them to guard holiness and the grace of God. The story of Esau, found in Genesis 25, is a warning. Some believe that "fornicator" also refers to Esau, but the biblical text does not say this clearly.

Today, we can ask ourselves what valuable things from God we are exchanging for a passing desire. Before giving in to a quick pleasure, it is wise to remember what truly matters and to ask God for strength to decide with wisdom.
exp.10:3:
This verse says that Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain, and that he did so by faith. Because of that faith, God declared him righteous and approved his offerings. The word "offerings" here means gifts. Although Abel died, his example still speaks to us.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers who needed to persevere. In chapter 11 he presents people from the Old Testament who trusted God. Abel is the first on the list. The text stresses that his offering was better because of his faith, not only because of what he offered. Genesis 4 tells the story, though it does not explain in detail why God accepted one offering and not the other.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our service to God springs from trust in Him or only from habit. God looks at the heart. We can offer Him our time, work, and worship with sincerity and faith.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that God himself backed up the message of salvation given by the first witnesses. He did this with signs (deeds that point to something beyond themselves), with miracles (works of power), and with wonders (things that cause amazement). He also did it with gifts of the Holy Spirit, that is, gifts that he distributed as he willed.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were in danger of neglecting their faith. He reminds them that the salvation announced by Jesus was confirmed by those who heard him, and that God himself gave testimony that this message is true. For that reason it should not be taken lightly.

Today we can take the gospel seriously and not treat it as something already known. God has backed it up with firmness, so it is worth listening to it carefully, obeying it, and giving thanks for the gifts that he gives his people to serve others.
exp.11:13:
It says we should earnestly pursue peace with everyone, and also holiness. "Follow" means to pursue, to strive to attain something. "Holiness" is living set apart for God, with a clean life dedicated to Him. The text affirms that without it, no one will see the Lord.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians weary from trials. He asked them to lift their drooping hands and walk with steady steps so that the weak might be healed. Then he warns them against bitterness and against living like Esau, who despised what was valuable for a bowl of food. Christians understand this holiness in different ways: as the fruit of Christ's work, as a path of growth, or both.

Today we can choose one concrete step: asking forgiveness from someone or forgiving someone, and praying that God will make us more like Jesus.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that Christ did not give himself the honor of being high priest. It was God who called him, saying to him: "You are my Son; today I have become your Father." The word "high priest" means the chief priest. "Begotten" here speaks of the Son's unique relationship with the Father, and it is taken from Psalm 2:7.

The writer of Hebrews explains that no priest appoints himself, as in the case of Aaron. God calls him. In this way he shows that Jesus is a legitimate priest, since his office comes from God and not from his own ambition. Who wrote Hebrews is not known with certainty, but the message is addressed to believers with a Jewish background.

For today: Jesus did not seek his own honor, but obeyed the Father's call. We can ask God to teach us to serve without seeking applause, trusting that his calling and his approval are worth more than any human recognition.
exp.11:1:
It says that, while we run the race of faith, we must keep our eyes fixed on Jesus. He is the "author," that is, the one who begins our faith, and the "finisher," the one who brings it to its goal. For the joy that lay ahead of him, he endured the cross and did not let himself be overcome by the shame it carried. Today he is seated at the right hand of God's throne.

The author of Hebrews does not identify himself; his name is not known with certainty. He writes to believers who are weary and tempted to give up because of pressure and suffering. Earlier he mentions the heroes of faith in chapter 11, and now he points to Jesus as the greatest example.

When you feel exhausted or ashamed for following Christ, do not look only at your problems. Set aside a moment each day to think about what Jesus suffered and about the hope he had. That renews your strength to keep going forward.
exp.10:23:
The explanation says that Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. That is, he turned down the privileges of belonging to the royal family of Egypt. He did this by faith, trusting God more than his own position.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were facing pressure and suffering. He presents them with examples of people from the Old Testament who trusted God. Moses appears alongside Joseph and his own parents. The verses that follow explain his decision: he chose to share the suffering of God's people, looking forward to a future reward.

Today, faith can lead us to give up advantages, comforts, or social approval if they draw us away from God. Ask yourself: is there something I am holding on to that keeps me from being faithful? With God's help, we can choose what is eternal over what is immediate.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that when God presents his Firstborn to the world, he commands that all the angels worship him. "Firstborn" is a title of honor and authority; it does not mean that Jesus was created. "Worship him" means: give him honor and reverence.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is superior to the angels. The quotation seems to come from passages such as Deuteronomy 32:43 (in the ancient Greek version) or Psalm 97:7. Scholars do not agree on whether "when he brings" refers to his birth, his resurrection, or his return.

For today: if the angels worship Jesus, we too can do so. Give him first place today in your decisions and in your gratitude.
exp.1:7:
He says that God put everything under the rule of human beings, so that nothing was left outside that rule. But the author admits a reality: we do not yet see everything made subject to humanity. "Thou hast put in subjection" means "you put under authority," and "put under him" means "placed under him."

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself in the text, quotes Psalm 8 to write to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus, made human, fulfills what that psalm promises. Although today the world seems disordered, the next verse points to Jesus, crowned with glory after suffering death.

When life seems out of control, remember that Jesus is already crowned and that the end of history is in God's hands. You can wait with patience and confidence, praying and obeying today.
exp.2:16:
This verse asks a question in order to answer it right away: with whom was God angry for forty years? With those who sinned, that is, those whose bodies fell dead in the wilderness.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to believers who were tempted to lose heart. He cites Psalm 95 and reminds his readers of the people of Israel who left Egypt, distrusted God, and died in the wilderness before entering the promised land. He uses this as a warning to his readers.

For today: when God speaks to you through his Word, do not delay your response or let your heart grow hard little by little. Trust him and obey him today, even when the road is long or difficult.
exp.11:26:
This verse says that the words "Yet once more" announce a change: God will remove the things that can be shaken, that is, the created things, so that what is firm will remain. "Shaken" means moved or made to tremble, and what can be shaken is anything that can be moved or disturbed.

The writer of Hebrews quotes the prophet Haggai (2:6) and warns believers not to refuse God when he speaks. When God spoke at Sinai, the earth shook. Now he speaks from heaven, and the warning is even more serious. Many understand that the kingdom of God is the only thing that cannot be shaken, although interpreters debate exactly how this will be fulfilled.

For today: do not place your security in things that can fall, such as money, work or reputation. Rest on Christ and on his kingdom, and respond to his voice with gratitude and reverence.
exp.5:9:
This verse says that God is righteous and does not forget what you have done. He remembers your work and the labor of love you showed toward his name, by helping the saints, that is, the believers, and by continuing to help them still.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers who were tired and tempted to give up. First he gives them a serious warning, but then he calls them dear friends and tells them he expects better things from them. This verse encourages them: their service has value to God. Then he invites them to keep going steadily to the end, with faith and patience.

For today: do not underestimate simple, steady service, such as visiting someone who is sick, helping a brother or sister, or serving in your church without applause. God sees it and remembers it. Be encouraged to keep serving with love, without growing weary.
exp.0:6:
The verse says that God makes his angels "spirits," that is, spiritual beings, and that his "ministers," or servants, he makes into a flame of fire. The word "spirits" can also be understood as "winds." Both ideas show that the angels are powerful, but that their role is to serve.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, quotes Psalm 104:4 here. He writes to believers with a Jewish background and wants to show that Jesus is superior to the angels. The angels are servants of God, but the next verse says that the Son is called God and is given an eternal throne.

Today, this text invites us to put Jesus first. The angels are a gift from God, but only Christ deserves our worship and trust.
exp.11:18:
Este versículo recuerda lo que pasó en el monte Sinaí. Allí sonó una trompeta y se oyó una voz que hablaba palabras. El pueblo se asustó tanto que pidió que Dios no les siguiera hablando.

El autor de Hebreos escribe a cristianos de origen judío que se sentían tentados a volver a la antigua forma de vida. Les muestra cómo fue la experiencia de Israel con la ley: algo temible, con fuego, oscuridad y distancia. Lo hace para contrastarla con lo que ahora tienen en Cristo, que describe poco después como acercarse al monte Sión, no al Sinaí.

Para hoy: Dios es santo y merece respeto, pero en Cristo podemos acercarnos a Él con confianza. Hoy puedes orar sin miedo, con reverencia y gratitud, recordando que Jesús abrió el camino.
exp.10:21:
It says that Joseph, when he was about to die, believed that God would keep his promise to bring Israel out of Egypt. The word "departing" in the verse refers to the people's leaving. The phrase "gave commandment" means that he gave an order: that his bones be carried with them to the promised land.

The writer of Hebrews goes through examples of faith from the Old Testament. Joseph lived in Egypt as a ruler, but he did not cling to that place. According to Genesis 50:24-25, he trusted that God would visit his people. Later, Exodus 13:19 tells that Moses carried his bones. The text gives no further details about how Joseph understood all of this.

For today: faith not only helps us live in the present, it also looks ahead with confidence in God's promises. Even if you have comfort or success here, remember that your final hope is in God. Live and plan in such a way that your decisions show that confidence.
exp.12:18:
The author asks for prayer with even more insistence: "But I beseech you the rather to do this," meaning that they should pray for him and his companions. The reason is that he may be restored to them the sooner.

The author of Hebrews does not give his name, and we do not know for certain who he was. He writes to a Christian community that he knows and from which, for some reason, he is separated. The text does not explain the reason: it could be a journey, a hardship, or a prison. At the close of the letter, he asks for their prayers with humility and confidence, like someone who needs the support of his brothers and sisters.

Today we can learn that praying for one another is a real act of love and unity. Think of someone in your church, or a pastor, who is far away or going through a trial. Pray for that person by name today, and if you can, let them know you did.
exp.10:36:
It says that many believers suffered terrible things for their faith: they were killed by stoning, sawn in two, or put to the sword. Here, "tempted" probably means put to the test, perhaps tempted to deny their faith. Others wandered covered in sheepskins and goatskins, without a home, poor, distressed and mistreated.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named and whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to tired believers who were under pressure. In chapter 11 he goes through a list of heroes of the faith.
