Here he shows that faith does not always bring immediate relief; sometimes it costs a great deal. Even so, the text that follows says the world was not worthy of them.

Today, if your faith brings you mockery, loneliness or hardship, do not think God has abandoned you. Remember that others have walked that road and God counted them as precious. Keep trusting, one day at a time.
exp.6:20:
This verse compares the priests of the Old Testament with Jesus. The Levites became priests without God making an oath. Jesus, however, was made priest with an oath. God himself said to him: "The Lord swore, and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever." "Forever" means for all time, and "will not change his mind" means that God will not change his purpose.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers of Jewish background, who were probably tempted to return to the law and its sacrifices. He quotes Psalm 110:4 to show that the priesthood of Jesus is superior: it is backed by God's solemn promise and does not depend on a family line. Who wrote the letter is not known with certainty.

For today: your relationship with God rests on a Priest whom God himself confirmed with an oath. When you doubt your forgiveness, remember that his commitment does not change. Draw near to God with confidence, relying on Jesus and not on your performance.
exp.5:18:
This verse says that the hope we have in God is like an anchor for the soul: sure and firm. The veil was the curtain of the temple that separated the Most Holy Place, where God's presence was. The high priest is the one who entered there once a year, and the forerunner is the one who goes ahead to open the way.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who are tired and tempted to give up. He reminds them that God made a promise and confirmed it with an oath. Two things that do not change, God's promise and his oath, give strong comfort. This hope reaches all the way into God's presence, because Jesus has already entered there for us as high priest.

For today: when storms come, such as sickness, fear, or uncertainty, do not lean on your feelings, which change. Pray and remember a specific promise of God, and rest in the fact that Jesus is already where you long to arrive.
exp.10:0:
This verse says that faith is like a firm foundation for what we still hope for, and a proof of what we cannot see with our eyes. The words "substance" and "evidence" in the verse point to something solid and sure, and to conviction or proof. In other words, faith gives us inner certainty about God's promises, even though we have not yet seen them fulfilled.

The author of Hebrews is not identified with certainty; several names have been proposed, but no one knows for sure. He writes to believers who are tired or tempted to give up, and he wants to encourage them to trust God. This verse opens the chapter of the heroes of faith: people from the Old Testament who trusted God without seeing everything fulfilled.

Today, when you face an uncertain situation, such as an illness, a debt, or a long wait, you can lean on what God has already promised and shown. Pray, and take the next step with confidence, even though you cannot see the whole path.
exp.0:11:
God says that he will do with the heavens and the earth what is done with an old cloak: he will fold them up, and they will be changed. The words "fold up" and "changed" are the ones to note here. In contrast, the Son remains the same, and his life never comes to an end.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 102 and applies it to the Son, that is, to Jesus. He wants to show his readers, believers of Jewish background who may have felt pressure to turn back, that Christ is superior to the angels. The angels serve, but the Son is eternal and created all things. Scholars agree that the central theme is the greatness of Christ.

Today, when everything changes, the news, our health, or our work, you can rest in someone who does not change. When you feel that something is wearing out or being lost, pray and give it to Jesus, and trust that his faithfulness lasts forever.
exp.10:8:
By faith Abraham lived in the land God had promised him, but as a foreigner would. He had no permanent home; he lived in tents, which were temporary shelters. His son Isaac and his grandson Jacob did the same. The phrase about being "heirs with him of the same promise" means that all three received the same promise from God.

The author of Hebrews is unknown, and tradition has debated who he was. He writes to Jewish believers who were tired and tempted to give up. He gives them examples of faith from people of the past. Abraham believed a promise that he did not see fulfilled in his lifetime, and the verse that follows says he was looking forward to an eternal city, built by God.

For today: we can live with patience when God's promises take a long time. We do not have to cling to what is temporary, because our firmest hope is in God. Trust Him and keep obeying today.
exp.7:12:
He says that, by speaking of a "new covenant," God declared the first one "old." And what becomes old and wears out with the years is close to vanishing.

The writer of Hebrews addresses believers with a Jewish background. He has just quoted the promise from Jeremiah 31 about a covenant in which everyone would know God and their sins would be forgiven. His argument is that God himself announced something new, and this shows that the first covenant was not the final stage of the plan. Scholars debate how to connect this with the destruction of the temple in the year 70, but the text does not say so clearly.

Today we can rest in Christ, not in our achievements or rituals. If God promises forgiveness and a close relationship, we can come to him with confidence, without fear that our past will disqualify us.
exp.0:9:
It says that the Lord was the one who, in the beginning, laid the foundations of the earth, and that the heavens are the works of his hands. The word "laid" means that you set in place or established a firm base. The phrase "in the beginning" points to the origin of creation.

The writer of Hebrews is showing that Jesus, the Son, is superior to the angels. Here he quotes Psalm 102:25-27, a psalm addressed to God, and applies it to the Son. In this way he affirms that Christ is not a creature, but took part in creation. Some scholars debate how the psalm was applied, but the general meaning in the letter is clear: the Son is Creator and is eternal.

For today: if Christ made all things and remains when everything changes, you can trust him in the midst of uncertainty. When you feel that nothing is secure, pray and entrust your worries to the One who sustains the universe and does not change.
exp.6:13:
It says that everyone knows that Jesus, our Lord, was born from the tribe of Judah. And Moses said nothing about priests from that tribe. "Evident" means clear and known to all. "Concerning" means "about." According to the law, priests came from the tribe of Levi, not from Judah.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is a different kind of priest, in the style of Melchizedek, and not in the style of Levi. If the priesthood changes, the law that supported it changes too. Jesus did not fit the old system, and that is why God was doing something new.

For today: you do not need a go-between or a special ritual to draw near to God. Jesus is your priest, and through Him you can pray with confidence, today, just as you are.
exp.7:7:
This verse says that God, while pointing out the failure of his people, announced that days would come when he would make a new covenant with Israel and Judah. The phrase "finding fault with them" means correcting them or pointing out their error.

The author of Hebrews quotes the prophet Jeremiah (31:31-34). He writes to believers of Jewish background and wants to show them that Jesus is the mediator of a better covenant than the one given through Moses. The problem did not lie in God's law, but in the fact that the people did not remain faithful. That is why God promised something new, one that reaches the heart.

For today: do not rely on your own strength to be faithful to God. He offers you a new relationship through Christ and can transform you from the inside. Ask him each day that his Word take root in your heart.
exp.8:24:
It says that Jesus did not enter heaven to offer himself over and over. The high priest, who in the Jewish temple entered the most holy place every year, went in with blood that was not his own, the blood of animals. Christ, by contrast, offered his own blood.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to return to the temple rites. He shows them that Christ is superior: the old system was a shadow of the good things to come, and Christ entered heaven itself, before God.

For today: you do not need to earn forgiveness through repeated efforts or live in fear of not having done enough. Jesus' sacrifice was complete. You can draw near to God with confidence and gratitude, and respond with a life of love and obedience, not of fear.
exp.3:11:
The explanation says that the word of God is not dead or weak, but living and powerful. It is sharper than any two-edged sword and reaches to the deepest part of a person. The phrase about piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, is a way of speaking about reaching the most inner parts of a person. It also speaks of discerning, that is, judging, the thoughts and intents of the heart.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers. He warns them not to repeat the disobedience of Israel in the wilderness, which lost the rest that was promised. The word of God is the voice that calls them to obey today.

For today: read the Bible with an open heart, letting God reveal your hidden motives. Ask Him to correct you with love and to help you obey.
exp.5:11:
Hebrews 6:12 tells us not to become lazy, meaning sluggish or idle in the life of faith. Instead, we should imitate those who, trusting God and waiting with patience, receive what God has promised. The word "inherit" means they receive it as a gift, not as a wage.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, is writing to Christians who had served with love but could grow weary. He has just encouraged them to keep the same diligence until the end. Then he points to Abraham, to whom God made a sure promise.

For today: when you feel weariness in your faith, do not give up. Choose one simple practice, such as praying each day or serving someone, and keep at it, trusting that God keeps what he promises.
exp.8:20:
The verse says that Moses also sprinkled with blood the tabernacle, that is, the sacred tent where Israel worshiped God, and all the vessels of the ministry, that is, the utensils used in worship. Nothing was left unset apart for God through the blood.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He explains that the first covenant was inaugurated with blood, and that this pointed to something greater: the sacrifice of Christ. The verses that follow affirm this: without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, but the heavenly realities required a better sacrifice.

Today we can remember that drawing near to God never depended on our effort or our rituals. Christ has already paid the price. You can pray with confidence, without carrying guilt that He has already covered.
exp.6:0:
This verse presents Melchisedec as king of Salem and priest of the Most High God. When Abraham was returning from defeating the kings who had taken his nephew Lot, Melchisedec went out to meet him and blessed him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He returns to the account in Genesis 14 to show that Christ is a priest of an order different from and superior to that of Aaron. Melchisedec appears suddenly in the story, and that is why he is used as a figure who points to Jesus.

For today: after a victory or an achievement, recognize that God is the one who sustains you. Receive the blessing of others with humility, and give thanks to God, our High Priest.
exp.9:17:
This verse says that when sins have already been completely forgiven, there is no need to offer another sacrifice to take them away. "Forgiveness" here means complete pardon, and "offering for sin" is the sacrifice that was brought to ask for that pardon.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself and whose identity is debated, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He has just quoted Jeremiah's promise about the new covenant, where God says he will remember their sins no more. His argument is that Jesus' sacrifice fulfilled that promise, so the repeated sacrifices in the temple are no longer necessary.

For today: if you have trusted in Christ, you do not have to live trying to earn forgiveness through your own efforts, guilt, or punishments. When you fail, come to God with sincerity and gratitude, not with fear, because Jesus has already paid what was necessary.
exp.9:33:
The verse says that the believers to whom this was written suffered along with the prisoners: the word "had compassion" means that they felt the pain of those who were in prison as if it were their own. They also accepted with joy the seizure of their possessions. Their joy came from knowing that they had an "enduring substance" that was better, meaning a treasure more valuable and lasting in heaven.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were going through hardships. He reminds them how brave they were at the beginning of their faith, to encourage them not to give up now and to keep their confidence until the end.

Today we can ask ourselves what we value most. When we place our security in what is eternal, it will be easier to be generous, to stand with those who suffer, and to bear losses with hope.
exp.8:27:
It says that Christ was offered once to take away, bear, or carry the sins of many. The text speaks of two comings: the first, to bear sin; the second, without sin, meaning without having to deal with sin again, because it has already been resolved. Then he will be seen by those who are waiting for him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to Christians with a Jewish background. He compares Christ with the sacrifices in the temple, which were repeated. He reminds his readers that people die once and then comes judgment; in the same way, Christ was offered once. His work is complete and does not need to be repeated.

For today: if Christ has already dealt with sin, you can draw near to God with confidence, without trying to earn his forgiveness through effort. And while you wait for his return, live with hope and peace, not with fear.
exp.8:12:
This verse speaks of the sacrifices of the Old Testament. The blood of bulls and male goats, and the ashes of a young cow sprinkled on those who were "unclean" (people who, according to the law, could not draw near to God), set them apart for God and cleansed them on the outside, in the ceremonial sense. The phrase "sanctifies for the purifying of the flesh" shows that this effect was external.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background. He wants to show them that the old was real but limited. This verse sets up a comparison: if that cleansed on the outside, the next verse says how much more the blood of Christ will do, cleansing from within.

For today: you do not have to strive to earn forgiveness through rituals or merits. Draw near to God with confidence, because Christ can cleanse your conscience from guilt and give you freedom to serve him.
exp.9:14:
This verse says that the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us about what the author has just explained. The phrase that means "bears witness to us" can also be rendered as "confirms it to us." Then the text introduces a quotation from Scripture with the words "for after that he had said before," and the quotation continues in the following verses.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to believers of Jewish background. He explains that Christ's sacrifice was sufficient and complete. To support this, he quotes the promise of the new covenant from Jeremiah 31, and he says that the Holy Spirit speaks through those ancient words.

For today: when you doubt that God has truly forgiven you, return to what his Word says. The Spirit confirms that Christ's work is enough, and you can rest in that promise without trying to earn forgiveness.
exp.3:7:
It says that Joshua could not give the people true rest from God. If he had, Psalm 95 would not have spoken centuries later of another day to enter that rest. "Would have given them rest" means he would have brought them into complete rest. Here Joshua is the same name as Jesus in Greek, but the reference is to the Joshua who led Israel into the promised land.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers tempted to abandon their faith. He reminds them that Israel entered Canaan, yet David, long afterward, still spoke of a rest yet to come. In this way he shows that the promise pointed to something deeper than a land: rest in God himself.

For today: do not look for lasting peace in achievements, places, or human help. When you are weary, listen today to the voice of God and trust in Christ, who offers a rest that nothing in this world can give.
exp.2:15:
This verse reminds us that some of the people God brought out of Egypt, although they heard his voice, provoked him, that is, they offended him by rebelling against him. Some translations read it as a question: "Who were those who, having heard, provoked him? Were they not all those who came out of Egypt?" The text allows both readings.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, quotes Psalm 95 and recalls the rebellion of the people in the wilderness, as told in Numbers 14. He writes to believers tempted to abandon their faith, and he warns them with an example from Israel's history.

For today: having seen God's work is not enough if we stop trusting and obeying. Today, when you sense that God is speaking to you through his Word, respond with humility and obedience instead of putting it off or hardening your heart.
exp.12:24:
It says that grace, that is, God's undeserved favor and help, be with all the readers. "Amen" means "so be it." The second phrase, "Written to the Hebrews from Italy by Timothy," is a note added at the end in some ancient manuscripts. It is not part of what the author wrote.

The author of Hebrews does not name himself, and we do not know for certain who he was. He closes the letter with a simple greeting and a wish for blessing on the whole community. That final note about Italy and Timothy is a later tradition and cannot be verified. What is clear is that he writes with pastoral care to believers who needed to persevere.

For today: when you say goodbye to someone, truly bless them. You can offer a brief prayer or a word of encouragement, remembering that we live by God's grace and not by our own strength.
exp.12:22:
He says that Timothy, the fellow worker, "is set at liberty," meaning that he has been released from prison. He notes that if Timothy comes soon, he will go with him to visit you.

The author of Hebrews does not name himself, and we do not know for certain who he was. He writes to Christians of Jewish background who faced pressure and weariness in their faith. It is not known when or where Timothy was imprisoned; the text only says that he has now been released. This closing note shows personal affection after a very deep letter.

For today: faith is lived out in real relationships. Share good news about your brothers and sisters, pray for those who suffer, and stay in touch with them. A phone call or a visit can encourage someone more than you might imagine.
exp.0:3:
He says that Jesus, the Son of God, is far superior to the angels. The word "excellent" means better, greater. "Obtained by inheritance" means that he received this place as a right of the Son. The more excellent "name" is "Son," which God never gave to any angel.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known with certainty, writes to Christians of Jewish background. They held the angels in great respect, since they believed God gave the law through them. The author wants to show that Christ is greater than all that came before, and for that reason it is worth following him with firmness, even in the midst of difficulties.

When life becomes hard or you feel tempted to look for support in other things, remember who Jesus is: the Son, the one who upholds all things and cleansed your sins. Trust in him above all.
exp.12:9:
We Christians, the explanation says, have an altar of our own, that is, a sacrifice and an offering that belong to us, and those who keep serving in the tent of worship of the old system have no right to take part in it. "Right" means permission or entitlement. The "tent of worship" was the place of worship in the Old Testament.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to return to laws about food and rituals. Earlier he had urged them not to be carried away by strange teachings. Many understand the "altar" to refer to Christ and his cross; others think of a broader idea of Christ's work. The verses that follow connect it with Jesus, who suffered outside the gate.

Today, do not look for your spiritual security in rituals, rules, or practices added to Christ. Rest in his complete sacrifice, and let his grace steady your heart.
exp.5:17:
He tells us that God gives us a very strong comfort based on "two things that cannot change," that is, his promise and his oath. It is impossible for God to lie. This encourages those who have fled for refuge, to take hold firmly of the hope that is offered to us.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not mentioned and whose identity is debated, writes to believers who are weary and tempted to abandon their faith. He reminds them that God made a promise to Abraham and confirmed that promise with an oath. In this way he wants to give them assurance that their hope in Christ is not fragile.

For today: when you feel doubt or fear, do not rely on your feelings, which change. Take a promise of God, read it aloud, and pray with it, holding on to it as to a firm rope.
exp.9:13:
It says that Jesus, through one sacrifice (his death on the cross), accomplished something complete and lasting. The phrase "perfected" means that he brought them to their goal, making them ready to stand before God. "Sanctified" refers to those who have been set apart for God.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known with certainty, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He compares the temple sacrifices, which were always being repeated, with Christ's single sacrifice. He wants to encourage them not to turn back. Then he quotes the new covenant, where God writes his law on the heart.

For today: if you trust in Christ, your relationship with God does not depend on your efforts or on starting over each day. Rest in what he has already done, and live thankful, letting God keep transforming your heart.
exp.11:8:
Verse 9 says that if we respected our human fathers when they corrected us, we should all the more submit ourselves to God, the Father of spirits. The word "corrected" here means those who corrected or disciplined us, not only those who punished us. "Respected" means we honored them with reverence. "Live" speaks of the true life that God gives.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who are tired from trials and pressure. He explains that difficulties may be the discipline of a Father who treats them as his children. He wants to encourage them not to give up. The verses that follow say this correction seeks our good and produces the fruit of righteousness.

Today, when you go through a difficulty, do not ask only "Why is this happening to me?" but also "What is God wanting to teach me?" Pray with humility and obey what He shows you, trusting that He corrects you with love.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that Jesus did not come to help the angels, but the descendants of Abraham. The word "took" here means to take by the hand to help and rescue. The "seed of Abraham" are the people who have faith, as Abraham did.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus truly became human, with flesh and blood, to defeat death and free those who lived in fear. That is why he can be a compassionate high priest.

When you feel that no one understands your struggle or your fear, remember that Jesus became one of us. He knows temptation and pain from experience, and He helps you up close. Draw near to Him in prayer with confidence.
exp.4:5:
This verse quotes another passage of Scripture (Psalm 110:4) to show that God himself appointed Christ as priest. "For ever" means forever, without end. "After the order of Melchisedec" means that his priesthood is like that of Melchisedec, a king and priest from the time of Abraham, and not like that of Aaron.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) is writing to believers of Jewish background. He explains that Jesus did not give himself the office of high priest, but that God called him to it. First he cites Psalm 2:7, and then Psalm 110:4, to confirm that calling.

For today: you can trust that Jesus serves as priest on your behalf forever. His help does not end and does not depend on you, so draw near to God in prayer with confidence, without fear.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that we who have believed do enter into God's rest. The phrase "as I have sworn in my wrath" means that God made a solemn promise of judgment, and the word "although" here marks a contrast. Those who did not believe would not enter that rest. And this is so even though God's works were finished from the creation of the world.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who could become discouraged. He quotes Psalm 95, where God spoke about the people of Israel in the wilderness, who did not enter the promised land because of their lack of faith. The author warns that the promise still stands and that hearing it is not enough: it must be believed.

Today, faith is not only hearing the Word, but trusting in it. If you are tired of struggling to earn God's favor, rest in what Christ has done and keep trusting in Him each day.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that the blood of Christ has a power far greater than the blood of animals. Christ offered himself to God "without spot," that is, without sin. "Through the eternal Spirit" can be understood as the Holy Spirit or as the divine nature of Christ; there are different opinions. His sacrifice cleanses the conscience from "dead works," which are actions that do not lead to life with God, so that we may now serve the living God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish origin. He explains that the sacrifices in the temple only purified the outward, but Christ offers an inner and lasting cleansing.

For today: if you carry guilt from your past, bring it to God with confidence. Christ has already paid for you, so you can let go of shame and serve God with a clear conscience.
exp.8:15:
This verse says that where there is a will, the death of the one who made it must be established. The person who leaves an inheritance is the one who made the will, and the death of that person must take place for the will to take effect.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that Christ is the mediator of the new covenant. The Greek word used here can be translated as "testament" or as "covenant," and scholars debate how it applies in this passage. In either case, the central idea is that Jesus' death makes possible the promised eternal inheritance.

Today we can receive salvation as a gift, not as a wage we earn. This week, thank God for what Christ has done, and live with the confidence of someone who has already been included in the inheritance.
exp.10:29:
This verse says that the walls of Jericho fell because the people of Israel trusted God. They walked around the city for seven days, just as God had told them. The word "faith" here means trusting and obeying, even when what is asked does not seem to make sense.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who are tired and tempted to give up. He shows them examples from the past: people who trusted God in difficult moments. He had spoken earlier about the Red Sea, and afterward he mentions Rahab. In this way he reminds them that God keeps what he promises.

For today: when God shows you a step you do not understand, obey it with patience, even if you do not see results right away. Sometimes faith looks like going around day after day, trusting that God will do his work in his own time.
exp.11:16:
It says that Esau, after selling his birthright, wanted to receive his father's blessing, but he was rejected. The word "rejected" here means turned away or cast off. Although he wept greatly, he found no way to change what he had already done, that is, he could not undo his choice.

The writer of Hebrews is addressing believers who were tired and tempted to abandon their faith. He uses Esau as a warning: Esau despised something sacred for the sake of a passing need. Interpreters debate whether the change of heart he could not find belonged to Esau or to Isaac, but all agree that his tears did not undo the consequences of his decision. It is a serious warning, not a rejection of anyone who seeks God sincerely.

Today we can ask ourselves what valuable parts of our faith we are trading away for comfort or fleeting desires. It is better to return to God today, with a humble heart, and to value what He has given us.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that in a certain place in Scripture the seventh day is spoken of, and that God rested from all his works on that day. The words "a certain place" refer to a passage the author quotes, in this case Genesis 2:2. The word "rested" means that God stopped his work of creation because it was already finished.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were tempted to give up their faith. He uses God's rest in creation to show that the rest he promises was already prepared from the beginning. He wants his readers not to be like the Israelites in the wilderness, who heard the promise but did not receive it with faith.

For today: God invites you to rest in what Christ has already done, without trying to earn his favor by your own effort. Today you can hand him one specific worry and trust that he cares for you.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that Jesus, while he lived as a man on earth ("in the days of his flesh"), offered prayers and supplications, with strong crying and tears, to God, who was able to save him from death. And he was heard because of his reverent fear, that is, his respectful awe and deep submission to God. "Was heard" does not necessarily mean that he was spared from dying, and scholars understand it in several ways.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named, explains why Christ is a true priest. A good priest understands human weakness. Many think this refers to Jesus' anguish in Gethsemane, although the text does not say so clearly.

We can pray with complete sincerity, even in tears, because Jesus knows pain. And we can trust that God hears us, even when his answer is different from what we asked for.
exp.9:26:
It says that for someone who deliberately rejects the truth of Christ, only a terrible judgment remains to be awaited. The word "horrible" here means dreadful, and "expectation" means an anticipation of what is coming, not something good. The "fierce burning fire" is an image of God's anger that will reach His "enemies," that is, those who oppose Him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians tempted to abandon their faith under pressure. He warns them that turning back after knowing Christ is rejecting the only sacrifice that forgives. Christians have debated whether he is speaking of true believers or of those who only seemed to be.

For today: do not walk away from the community or from Christ when everything gets hard. Seek the support of other believers, and if you have failed, return to Jesus with humility, for in Him forgiveness remains.
exp.10:18:
This verse says that Abraham reasoned that God has the power even to raise the dead. So, in a figurative sense, Abraham received Isaac back. The phrase "received him back" means that he got him back, and "in a figure" means like an image or example of the resurrection.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, speaks of Abraham's faith. God had promised him descendants through Isaac, and then asked him to offer him up (Genesis 22). Abraham trusted that God would keep his promise, even if that required a miracle as great as giving life back.

For today: when God asks you to trust in the middle of something you do not understand, remember his character and his promises. You can obey step by step, believing that he is faithful and powerful, even though you cannot yet see how he will resolve the situation.
exp.12:1:
This verse asks us not to stop welcoming others warmly, especially those who come from outside. The word "hospitality" here means love for the stranger, that is, opening your home and your table to someone who needs it. "Entertained angels" means they welcomed God's messengers into their homes without realizing it.

The author of Hebrews is not known for certain. He writes to Christians and, at the close of the letter, gives advice for daily life. This phrase explains how brotherly love is lived out. Many think it recalls Abraham and Sarah, and perhaps Lot, who received mysterious visitors, although the text does not name them.

Today you can invite someone new in your church to a meal, a lonely neighbor, or a migrant, without expecting anything in return.
exp.9:37:
The explanation says that the righteous person, that is, the one who is right with God, will live by trusting in Him. But if someone draws back, that is, turns away and abandons that trust, God takes no pleasure in that person. The phrase "my soul shall have no pleasure in him" means that God does not find joy in such a person.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who are tired and pressed by difficulties. Here he quotes the prophet Habakkuk (2:3-4), where God speaks. He reminds them that they need patience, that Christ will return soon, and that they must not give up. Then he encourages them by saying that they are not among those who draw back, but among those who persevere.

When you are tired of praying or of waiting for an answer, do not turn away from God. Take one simple step of trust today: pray, read a passage of the Bible, and tell Him that you still trust Him.
exp.3:0:
We should have a healthy fear, that is, a serious care. God still offers to enter his rest, and no one should be left outside. The word "seem" here means "appear" or "be found"; "come short" means that someone was left behind, without reaching it. The word "you" in this verse is the plural form, addressed to all of you.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish origin. He has just reminded them of Israel in the wilderness, who did not enter the rest because of their unbelief. He warns them not to repeat that mistake. It is debated whether the "rest" refers mainly to the Promised Land, to rest in Christ, or to future rest with God; the text seems to join these ideas together.

Today, do not take your faith for granted. Make time to listen to the Word and respond to it with trust and obedience, not just with your ears.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that every house has someone who built it, and that the one who created absolutely all things is God. The word translated here as "created" simply means "made." Here "house" is not only a building but the people or family of God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who felt pressure to turn back. He compares Moses, who was highly respected, with Jesus. Moses was faithful in God's house, but Jesus is the builder. Many understand that by saying God made all things, the author presents Christ with divine dignity.

For today: if God is the one who builds his house, your life and your faith rest in him, not in your own strength. Remain firm in trust and hope, even in difficult times.
exp.10:19:
It says that Isaac blessed his sons Jacob and Esau by trusting in God, not only in what he could see. His blessings spoke of the future: "things to come" means things that were going to happen. The old wording with the accent mark is an older way of spelling "a," and it is not needed here.

The author of Hebrews goes through the history of earlier believers to show how faith led them to trust God's promises. Here he speaks of Isaac, already an old man, when he blessed his sons (Genesis 27). That story was complicated, with deception within the family, but the text highlights that Isaac believed God would carry out his plan later on, and so he spoke about what was to come.

For today: we can bless and encourage our children and loved ones with words that express hope in God. Even when we cannot see the whole future, we can trust that God continues to guide his story.
exp.1:9:
It seemed fitting to God, for whom and by whom all things exist, to make Jesus perfect through suffering. Jesus is the "captain of their salvation," meaning the one who opens the way to our salvation and begins it. In this way God would bring many sons to glory. "Perfect" means brought to fullness, complete in his mission; it does not mean that Jesus had any sin to be corrected.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers tempted to abandon their faith. He has just spoken of Jesus, made a little lower than the angels and crowned because he suffered. He explains that the cross was not a failure but the path God chose. The next verse says that Jesus calls us brethren.

For today: when you suffer, remember that Jesus has already walked that road and does not leave you alone. Your pain does not mean God has forgotten you; it can draw you closer to the One who leads you to his glory.
exp.10:5:
It says that without faith no one can please God. Whoever comes to Him must believe two things: that God exists, and that He rewards those who seek Him.

The author of Hebrews is not identified with certainty; the Bible does not say who wrote it, and several names have been proposed. He writes to believers who were tempted to give up. He has just mentioned Enoch, of whom it is said that he pleased God, and now he explains the reason: he did so by faith. Then he goes on with Noah and Abraham as examples of trust in God.

For today: when you pray, come trusting that God hears you and is good, even if you do not yet see an answer. Continuing to seek Him with perseverance is a simple way of living out faith.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that Jesus speaks about God to his brothers and sisters. "I will declare" means to make known, and "thy name" stands for who God truly is. "The church" is the gathered assembly, and "will I sing praise" means to sing or speak with gratitude and honor.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 22:22 and places these words on the lips of Christ. It follows from saying that Jesus is not ashamed to call those he makes holy "brothers." Many understand that Jesus, by becoming human and suffering, joins himself to his people and leads their worship. The psalm begins in anguish but ends in praise, and so it fits the theme of suffering that leads to glory.

Today you can remember that Jesus considers you part of his family and that, when you praise with other believers, you are not singing alone. Take part with joy in your church, and speak of how good God is with your family and friends.
exp.10:4:
This verse says that Enoch, by faith, was taken by God out of this world without passing through death. They no longer found him, because God had taken him. The word "translated" that appears in the verse means carried over from one place to another. "Was not found" means that they searched for him and he did not appear. Before he was taken, it was said of him that he pleased God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers to encourage them to persevere. He presents examples of faith from the Old Testament: Abel, then Enoch, then Noah. Genesis 5:24 tells that Enoch walked with God. The following verse explains that without faith it is impossible to please God.

For today: pleasing God is not a matter of doing extraordinary things, but of walking with Him each day, trusting that He exists and rewards those who seek Him. Today you can set aside a few minutes to speak with Him and entrust Him with your day.
exp.10:37:
This verse says the world did not deserve these faithful believers. Although people treated them as if they were disposable, God saw them as very precious. They lived fleeing through deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the earth.

The author of Hebrews (we do not know for certain who he was) writes to believers who were weary and tempted to give up. He shows them a list of people of faith who suffered greatly. The verses that follow say that they waited for God's promise and did not see it fulfilled in full, because God had something better prepared for everyone.

For today: if you face rejection or hardship for following Christ, remember that the world does not define your worth. God sees your faithfulness and invites you to keep trusting, without giving up.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that the tabernacle and its rituals were a picture, that is, an image or example, of that time before Christ. The gifts were the offerings, and the sacrifices were the animals brought. None of it could make the worshiper complete in regard to the conscience, that is, it could not cleanse the inside or take away the guilt of the heart.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that the tabernacle system pointed to something greater. He explains this so that they do not turn back, for in Christ they have what those rites only foretold.

For today: if your conscience accuses you of past failures, do not try to quiet it with your own efforts or rituals. Bring it to Christ, who can truly cleanse the heart, and rest in his forgiveness.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that the blood of animals, such as bulls and male goats, has no real power to take away the sins of people. Here "take away" means to remove or set aside guilt completely. The sacrifices of the law showed how serious sin is, but they could not truly cleanse the conscience at its root.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that the sacrifices offered again every year in the temple pointed to something better. He is preparing them to present Christ, who, through his offered body, dealt with the problem of sin once and for all.

For today: we do not have to carry guilt, trying to make up for our mistakes through efforts, rituals, or good works. We can draw near to God with sincerity, confess our sin, and rest in the forgiveness that Jesus has already won for us.
exp.9:31:
This verse invites readers to remember the past. "But" is the word used here in place of "Empero," and "illuminated" refers to those who had understood and received the truth of Christ. After that moment, they endured a great fight of afflictions, that is, a long and hard struggle with many sufferings.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who are weary and tempted to abandon their faith. Earlier he had warned them firmly about the danger of turning away from God. Now he gently reminds them that they have already endured difficult trials, to encourage them not to give up.

For today: when you feel weary in the faith, remember how God sustained you in hard moments. Write down some of those experiences and thank Him for them. That remembrance can give you strength to keep trusting Him today.
exp.11:28:
It says God is like a consuming fire. This is an image, not a literal description. Fire burns up what cannot withstand it, and it also purifies. The word "consuming" means that it destroys completely whatever it reaches. In this way, the text shows the holiness of God, who does not tolerate evil.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to Christians who are tempted to turn back. He reminds them that everything that can be shaken will be shaken, but the kingdom of God stands firm. For this reason he asks them to serve God with reverence and awe, that is, with deep respect and gratitude. The phrase seems to draw on images from the Old Testament, such as Deuteronomy 4:24.

Today, do not take God lightly. Come to Him with humility and gratitude, and ask Him to burn away in you pride, sin, and everything that does not last. His fire, in Christ, seeks to cleanse you and not to destroy you.
exp.7:3:
It says that if Jesus were here on earth, he would not even be a priest, because there are already priests who offer the gifts according to the law of Moses. The word "gifts" here means the offerings or gifts that were brought to God. Jesus did not belong to the tribe of Levi, which was the tribe of the priests.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus serves in a heavenly sanctuary, not in the earthly temple. His priesthood is different and superior, and so it does not compete with the old system.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus intercedes for us in God's presence. We do not need to seek other intermediaries or depend on rituals to draw near. We can pray with confidence, knowing that our High Priest understands us and welcomes us.
exp.6:10:
This verse asks a question: if the priesthood of Levi, with its law and its sacrifices, could bring a person to perfection (that is, to a complete and true relationship with God, with sin truly dealt with), why did God announce another priest, after the order of Melchisedec and not of Aaron?

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He has just shown that Melchisedec is greater than Levi, because Abraham gave him a tenth. His point is that the Levitical priesthood was not enough, and that is why God promised another (Psalm 110:4).

For today: do not trust your efforts, rituals, or good behavior to make you right with God. Rest in Jesus, our high priest, who can truly give us full access to God.
exp.6:17:
The explanation says that the earlier commandment, that is, the law that organized the Levitical priesthood, is set aside or put to one side. The reason is that it was weak and could not accomplish what it promised. The word the verse uses for this setting aside means that it is cancelled or no longer has effect.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and whom scholars debate, writes to believers of Jewish background who may have wanted to return to the old ways. He has just shown that Jesus is a priest in the order of Melchizedek, not by human descent. For that reason he explains that the earlier system could not bring people into a full relationship with God, and that Christ brings a better hope.

For today: do not trust your religious efforts, routines, or merits to make you feel accepted by God. Draw near to Him with confidence, resting on Jesus, who lives forever and opens the way for us.
exp.12:3:
Hebrews 13:4 says that marriage should be held in high esteem by everyone, and that the intimacy within it is pure, without blame. On the other hand, God will judge those who live in sexual immorality (fornicators) and those who betray their marriage (adulterers). The phrase "bed without stain" means a bed without blemish. The word "honourable" means worthy of honour.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, closes his letter with practical instructions for Christian life. Earlier he speaks of hospitality and of caring for prisoners; afterward, of money and trust in God. In this way, faithfulness in marriage appears as part of a life given over to God.

Today we can honour marriage by being faithful in actions and thoughts, speaking respectfully of our spouse, and caring for mutual trust. If you are single, you can also honour marriage by living with purity and supporting the married couples around you.
exp.9:27:
It says that under the law of Moses, a person who openly looked down on it and was accused by two or three witnesses died without anyone showing them pity. "Looked down on" means rejecting something or giving it little value. "Without any mercy" means that once the wrongdoing was proven, the punishment was not eased.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to abandon Christ. He reminds them how serious it was to disobey the old law, to show that rejecting Christ, who is greater than Moses, is even more serious. The verses that follow make this comparison. Scholars debate how to understand the "willful sin" in the previous verse, but all of them see here a warning against deliberately turning away from Christ.

Today, do not take God's grace lightly. If you have felt the urge to step away from Christ, return to Him with humility and value what it cost to be forgiven.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that the people of Israel could not enter the promised land, here called "his rest," for one clear reason: they did not believe. The phrase "because of" means "on account of" or "by reason of," and the word "because" in the King James reading points to the same cause. The unbelief here is not just doubt, but not trusting God, and that led to not obeying him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were tempted to give up. He reminds them of what happened to the generation that left Egypt with Moses and fell in the wilderness. He quotes Psalm 95 to warn them not to repeat that mistake.

Today we can ask ourselves in what area we are distrusting God. When he asks something of us and we feel afraid, faith shows itself by taking the next step of obedience, even a small one, trusting that he keeps what he promises.
exp.11:11:
This verse encourages weary believers to regain their strength. The phrase "lift up" means raising up, and "weak" describes knees that are feeble and loose, no longer holding a person up well. It is the picture of someone exhausted in a race.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who were going through hardships. He has just explained that God's discipline, though painful, is a sign that he treats us as his children and produces the peaceful fruit of righteousness. For this reason, the verse begins with "Therefore": since God corrects us for our good, we should not give up. The verses that follow call for walking straight and helping those who are lame.

For today: if you are tired from a trial, do not stay fallen. Take one small step today, pray, go to church, or seek out a brother or sister who can encourage you, and do the same for someone who is weak.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that the good news was preached to us too, just as it was to the people of Israel in the wilderness. But hearing the message did not help them, because they did not receive it with faith. The word "preached" means that the good news was given to us. The phrase "not being mixed with faith" means joining what is heard with real trust in God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were at risk of drifting away. He reminds them of the generation of the exodus, who heard God's promise about the land of rest but did not enter because of their unbelief. He warns them kindly not to repeat that mistake.

For today: hearing the Bible or attending church is not enough. Today you can choose one promise of God, trust it, and obey it in something concrete this week.
exp.6:11:
Here "changed" means altered, and "change" means alteration. The author states that if the priesthood is changed, the law that depended on it must also be changed. The law and the Levitical priesthood were closely bound together.

The book of Hebrews was addressed to believers with a Jewish background. Its author is unknown. Its purpose is to show that Jesus, of the tribe of Judah and a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, is superior to the priesthood of Aaron. If God appointed a new priest, He also established a new way of drawing near to Him. Christians understand in different ways how far this change in the law extends.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus is our priest. We do not need to earn God's favor through rituals. We can approach Him with confidence, through Christ.
exp.11:9:
It says that our earthly fathers corrected us for a short time, and they did so according to what seemed good to them, though they could make mistakes. God, on the other hand, always corrects us for our good, with a clear purpose: that we come to share in his holiness. Here "chastened" is understood as disciplining or training, not only as punishment.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who were tired from trials and tempted to give up. He reminds them that difficulties do not mean that God has abandoned them. On the contrary, they are a sign that he treats them as sons and is shaping them.

Today, when you go through a difficulty or a correction, do not ask only "Why me?" Also ask: "Lord, what do you want to teach me?" Trust that your Father does not correct you out of anger, but out of love, to help you grow.
exp.5:4:
This verse continues to describe people who have had real experiences with God. "They tasted the good word of God" means they tested and came to know his message up close. "The powers of the world to come" refers to the powers of the future, that is, the displays of God's power that point ahead to the world he will bring.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to tired believers who may have been tempted to abandon Christ. He warns them seriously about the danger of turning away. Christians have understood this passage in different ways: some see a real loss of salvation, others see a description of people who seemed to believe but did not have true faith.

For today: do not be content with having tasted the things of God. Feed your faith every day with the Bible, prayer, and fellowship with other believers.
exp.6:27:
This verse compares two kinds of priests. The law of Moses appointed men as high priests who were weak, with flaws and sins. But the word of the oath, which God spoke after the law (referring to Psalm 110:4), appoints the Son as priest. He was made complete and without fault forever, and his priesthood never ends.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to return to the system of priests and sacrifices. He shows them that Jesus is superior, because he does not need to offer sacrifices for his own sins, and his one offering was enough forever.

Today we can rest in the fact that our relationship with God does not depend on our own perfection or on that of any human leader. Jesus is a faithful and permanent priest. You can approach God with confidence, speaking to him in prayer, even when you feel weak.
exp.11:23:
It says that believers have come to Jesus, who is the Mediator, that is, the one who joins God and people through a new covenant (the word "testament" here means covenant). It also speaks of the "blood of sprinkling," which is blood that was sprinkled, as was done in the sacrifices. That blood speaks better than the blood of Abel.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to Jewish Christians tempted to give up. He compares Mount Sinai, full of fear, with the heavenly city of God. The blood of Abel cried out for justice (Genesis 4:10); the blood of Jesus speaks of forgiveness and reconciliation.

Today, when guilt accuses you, remember that the blood of Jesus speaks more loudly. Draw near to God with confidence, without fear, and listen to his voice.
exp.10:1:
The explanation says that believers of ancient times received God's approval because of their faith. "Obtaining a good report" means that God spoke well of them and approved them. "The elders" are the faithful men and women of Israel's past.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were going through trials and could feel tempted to give up their faith. After explaining what faith is, he begins to show examples from the Old Testament, such as Abel, to encourage them to keep trusting God.

For today: what God values in us is not perfection or success, but trust in Him. Today you can choose a difficult situation and say to God simply, "I trust You in this," and take the next step by obeying Him.
exp.1:8:
This verse says that we now see Jesus crowned with glory and honour. Before that, he was made "a little lower than the angels," meaning he took on human life for a time. He suffered death and, by the grace of God, "tasted death" for everyone, that is, he truly experienced it, on behalf of every person. "But" is the word that connects this part of the verse to what came before, and "suffering" refers to the pain he endured.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who needed encouragement. He has just quoted Psalm 8, which speaks of human beings placed over creation. He admits that we do not yet see everything made subject to them, but we do see Jesus, who passed through suffering before receiving glory.

For today: when you go through pain or trials, remember that Jesus knows suffering and lived through it out of love for you. Trust that God can lead your story toward hope, as He did with Him.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that the promise of entering God's rest is still open: it still remains that some must enter it. The first people who heard the good news, the people of Israel in the desert, did not enter because they disobeyed. "Since it remains" means "since it is still pending". "Was announced" means "was preached to them". "Disobedience" here means the same as not believing and not listening to God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to give up. He quotes Psalm 95 and Genesis to show that God's rest did not end with that generation. He warns them not to repeat the mistake of their ancestors.

For today: if you feel that God speaks to you through his Word, do not put it off. Respond with trust and simple obedience, today, in something concrete.
exp.9:18:
The explanation says that believers, whom the author calls "brethren," now have boldness to enter the holiest place, that is, the place where God himself is present. Boldness here means confidence and courage, not fear. And this entrance is possible through the blood of Jesus Christ, that is, through his death offered on our behalf.

The author of Hebrews (tradition is not unanimous about his name) has just explained that God forgave sins under the new covenant and that no more sacrifices are needed. With "Therefore" he moves from teaching to application: if forgiveness is complete, we can approach God without dread. Before, only the high priest entered the most holy place, and only once a year.

For today: when you feel unworthy or far from God, pray with confidence. Your access does not depend on your performance, but on what Christ has done for you.
exp.9:21:
The explanation says that we can approach God with sincerity, trusting fully in Him. It explains that the verse's wording means "let us come near." It also says that "full assurance" means firm confidence. It speaks of having the heart cleansed from a guilty conscience and the body washed with clean water. Many understand this as an image of baptism; others see it as a picture of spiritual purification in general.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to lose heart or turn back. He reminds them that Jesus, our great priest, opened a new way to God. Before, only the priest entered the most holy place. Now all of us can draw near through Christ.

For today: when you feel guilty or unworthy, do not turn away from God. Pray honestly, confess what weighs on your conscience, and trust that Jesus has already opened the door. Come near today, just as you are.
exp.11:27:
This verse says that believers receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken or destroyed. So when it speaks of holding on to grace, it means clinging to the favor of God that we have received. With that grace, we serve God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and godly fear, that is, with deep respect and awe before who he is.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers who were weary and tempted to turn back. He reminds them that at Sinai God's voice shook the earth, and that one day he will shake all that has been created. Only what is firm will remain: the kingdom of God.

For today: when everything around you seems unstable, rest in the fact that you belong to a secure kingdom. Respond with gratitude, serving God with a respectful heart in everyday life: your work, your family, and your decisions.
exp.6:22:
This verse says that under the old covenant there were many priests, one after another, because death kept them from continuing to serve. In this verse, "certainly" is the sense of the word, and "continue" means remaining in the office.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and who has been much debated, writes to believers with a Jewish background who valued the Levitical priesthood. He wants to show them that Jesus is superior. The ancient priests died and had to be replaced, but Jesus, according to the next verse, lives forever and has a priesthood that does not pass to another.

For today: you can draw near to God with confidence, knowing that your priest never leaves and will never be replaced. When you feel weak or guilty, pray without fear, because Jesus lives always to intercede for you.
exp.9:30:
It says that falling into the hands of the living God is a terrible thing, one that brings great fear. The word for "dreadful" means frightening or worthy of fear, and "falling into his hands" means facing his judgment. "The living God" reminds us that God is real, active, and sees everything.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to tired Jewish Christians who were tempted to turn back. He warns them that deliberately abandoning Christ and despising his sacrifice is very serious. He cites the Old Testament to remind them that God judges his people. Then, in the verses that follow, he encourages them to remember their faithfulness in the past.

For today: do not take God's grace lightly. Let your trust in Christ be sincere, and let reverent fear lead you to persevere, not to live in dread, because in Jesus we have secure access to God.
exp.10:38:
This verse says that all the heroes of faith mentioned in Hebrews 11 were approved by God, that is, God saw their faith and was pleased with them. Yet even so, they did not live to see the promise fulfilled. The phrase "obtained a good report" means they received a good testimony, and "the promise" refers to what God had promised, which would be fully realized in Christ and his salvation.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were suffering and might feel like giving up their faith. He reminds them of faithful people from the Old Testament who trusted God without seeing everything fulfilled. The following verse explains that God had something better prepared for all of them together.

For today: if you are still waiting for an answer from God, do not think that he has forgotten you. You can keep trusting, because faith does not depend on seeing everything fulfilled now, but on believing that God is faithful.
exp.6:23:
This verse says that Jesus, unlike other priests, lives forever. That is why his priesthood is "unchangeable": it does not change hands or pass to someone else. The word "but" introduces the contrast, and "continueth ever" means that he remains alive and steadfast.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known with certainty, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He compares Jesus with the priests of the Old Testament, who were many because death kept them from continuing to serve. Jesus, by contrast, rose again, and so his service never comes to an end. This supports the idea that he guarantees a better covenant.

Today we can rest in the fact that our relationship with God does not depend on people who fail or die, but on Christ, who is always present. When you feel weak or guilty, draw near to God with confidence and pray in the name of Jesus.
exp.9:38:
They say that believers are not among those who draw back and end up lost, but among those who keep trusting God and so save their soul. "Drawing back" means turning around or giving up. "Ruin" is total destruction. The life of the soul made secure is what is meant by the gain of the soul. "Faithful" here refers to those who have faith and trust.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were under pressure and mistreatment because of their faith. There was a risk that they would turn back. He quotes the prophet Habakkuk: the righteous shall live by faith, and God is not pleased with the one who draws back. Then he encourages his readers with confidence: they are not part of that group.

For today: when you grow tired or trials make you doubt, do not keep going on your own strength alone. Seek God in prayer, read his Word, and lean on brothers and sisters who encourage you. A small step of faith today helps you stay firm.
exp.10:25:
He says that Moses considered that suffering insult or contempt for the sake of Christ was worth more than all the treasures of Egypt. Your reader's verse says "reproach of Christ," so the explanation's word for insult will be rendered as "reproach" in the translation. The sentence explaining the old word is rewritten to match the verse: "reproach" means disgrace or shame. "Recompence" is reward. Moses looked ahead, waiting for the prize that God would give.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who faced pressure and rejection. He presents Moses to them as an example of faith. Some understand "the reproach of Christ" to mean that Moses suffered a disgrace similar to Christ's, or that he joined the people who would bring forth the Messiah. Interpreters explain it in several ways.

For today: when being faithful to Christ costs you a friendship, an easy gain, or a certain respect, remember that God sees and rewards. Ask yourself what you are valuing most, and decide with your eyes fixed on what is eternal.
exp.11:24:
It tells us to be careful not to refuse God when he speaks to us. "Refuse" means to reject or despise, and "escaped" means that they did not get away from the punishment. If the people of old did not get away when they rejected the one who spoke on earth, then much less will we escape if we reject the one who speaks from heaven.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were weary and tempted to turn back. He compares Moses and Sinai, where God spoke on earth, with Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant. Since his blood speaks better than the blood of Abel, his message deserves even more attention.

Today we can listen to God with humility every day, by reading his Word and obeying what he shows us, instead of putting it off or making excuses.
exp.5:5:
It says that it is impossible to bring back to repentance those who, after knowing so closely the blessings of God, have fallen away. The idea of falling away speaks of turning away from faith. To treat Christ with contempt, as if his sacrifice were worth nothing, is what the phrase about crucifying the Son of God again means. Public shame or insult is what the idea of disgrace before others refers to.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to Jewish believers who may have felt pressure to abandon Christ. He warns them firmly and then encourages them. Christians interpret this passage in various ways: some see a warning about losing salvation, others see a description of those who never truly believed.

Today it invites us to take our faith seriously and not treat it with indifference. If you feel yourself drifting away, return to Christ soon with humility, and nurture your spiritual life through prayer and community.
exp.1:1:
The explanation says that the law, the word given through angels, was firm and valid. For that reason, every transgression (rebelling against God) and every disobedience received a just punishment. The word "stedfast" in the verse means firm and reliable, and "recompence of reward" means the payment or consequence that was deserved.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself and whom we cannot identify with certainty, writes to believers who were tempted to drift away from the faith. He refers to the law of Moses, which according to Jewish tradition was given with the mediation of angels (also mentioned in Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19). He argues that if ignoring that word had consequences, then ignoring the message of Christ, which is greater, is even more serious.

Today, let us not take lightly what God has said to us in Christ. Make time to read the Bible and to obey it, so that you do not slowly drift away without noticing.
exp.6:24:
He is able to save completely and forever those who draw near to God through him. "Save to the uttermost" can be understood as saving fully, or to the very end. "Draw near" means to come close. And because Jesus lives forever, he intercedes, that is, he asks and speaks on their behalf before God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He compares Jesus with the ancient priests, who died and had to be replaced. Jesus, by contrast, lives forever, and his priesthood does not pass to another or come to an end. For that reason his help never stops.

Today you can come near to God with confidence, even when you feel weak or guilty. You do not depend on your own steadiness, but on Jesus, who lives and prays for you. When you pray, do so remembering that he is already interceding on your behalf.
exp.6:15:
He says that Jesus was not made priest by a human rule based on family or descent, which is what "carnal commandment" means. In the law of Moses, priests had to come from the tribe of Levi. Jesús was made priest by the power of a life that cannot be destroyed. "Endless" means that it never dies out or comes to an end.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus, from the tribe of Judah, is a different and greater priest, like Melchizedek. His priesthood does not depend on a lineage, but on his resurrection and his eternal life.

Today you can trust that your Savior lives and never stops interceding for you. Your relationship with God does not depend on your record or your merits, but on Christ, who lives forever.
exp.10:7:
What it says: Abraham heard God's call and obeyed. He went out toward a place that God would give him as an inheritance, that is, as a gift that would pass on to his descendants. He did this even though he did not know where he was going.

Context: The author of Hebrews, whose name is not stated in the text, writes to believers who needed to persevere. After saying that without faith it is impossible to please God, and after showing Noah as an example, he presents Abraham. His faith was not just an idea: it was shown in action, and by going out he left what was familiar to follow God's promise.

For today: You may not see the whole road, but God may ask you to take the next step. Trust his character, pray, seek wise counsel, and obey in what he has already shown you, even if you do not yet understand the rest.
exp.10:34:
Women received their dead back to life. Others were stretched out on the rack, a word that describes being tortured, probably on an instrument of torment. They did not accept being set free, meaning they refused to be saved by denying their faith, because they were looking forward to a better resurrection.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were under pressure and tempted to give up. He shows them examples of faith from the Old Testament. The cases of women bring to mind the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite woman, in the time of Elijah and Elisha. The cases of torture probably refer to the time of the Maccabees, though this is debated.

Today, this encourages us to stand firm when following God costs something. We can trust that God's hope is worth more than any momentary relief.
exp.12:17:
He says the author asks his readers to pray for him and for those who are with him. He states that they have a clear conscience, that is, they do not feel they are acting with bad intentions. Moreover, they want to live well, an old-fashioned expression meaning to live and behave in a correct, honest way in every area of life.

The author of Hebrews does not identify himself in the letter, and we do not know for certain who he was. He writes to a Christian community that he knows and wants to visit again, as the following verse indicates. After speaking about obeying the leaders, he now places himself as someone who needs prayer. His request shows humility: even teachers depend on the prayers of others.

For today: pray specifically for your pastors, teachers, or leaders, that they may live with integrity. And examine your own conscience: ask God to help you live honestly in your everyday life.
exp.2:0:
This verse invites believers, called "holy brethren" because God has set them apart for himself, to fix their attention on Jesus. It presents him as the one sent from God, the Apostle, and as the High Priest, the one who brings people together with God. The word "profession" here means the faith we confess, and "heavenly calling" is God's call that comes from heaven.

The writer of Hebrews does not identify himself in the text, and people have debated who he was. He writes to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to give up their faith. He then compares Jesus with Moses, whom they respected greatly, and shows that Jesus is greater, just as the builder is greater than the house.

For today: when you feel tired or doubtful, do not first look to your own strength or your problems. Set aside a few minutes each day to read about Jesus in the Gospels and to pray, remembering that he represents you before God.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that Jesus, after offering his sacrifice, is seated at the right hand of God and waits. The phrase "from henceforth expecting" refers to the time that remains until the end. "Footstool" was a small stool where the feet rested; placing enemies there means their total defeat.

The author of Hebrews compares the priests, who offered sacrifices again and again, with Christ, who offered one sacrifice for all time. That is why he has already sat down: his work is finished. Here the author draws on Psalm 110:1. His purpose is to encourage believers who were doubting, showing that Christ is superior and that his final victory is certain.

For today: you can rest in the fact that your forgiveness does not depend on your efforts, but on what Christ has already done. And although you see evil in the world, you can wait with patience and confidence, because God will fulfill his promise in his time.
exp.5:12:
This verse says that when God made a promise to Abraham, He swore by Himself, because there was no one greater than Him to swear by. Making a promise is one thing, and swearing is confirming with a solemn commitment that one is telling the truth and will keep it.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers who were growing weary in their faith. He asks them not to be lazy, but to imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and patience. He holds up Abraham as an example, reminding them that God confirmed His word with an oath, as seen in Genesis 22.

For today: when the waiting becomes long and you begin to doubt, remember that God does not only promise, but backs His word with His own character. You can rest in that and keep trusting with patience, one day at a time, praying and obeying.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that Jesus is not a distant or indifferent high priest. The word "high priest" is an older term here, meaning the one who brings people before God. The word "infirmities" refers to our weaknesses. Jesus understands what we feel, because he was tempted in every way as we are, yet he never sinned.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers who needed encouragement not to abandon their faith. Earlier he spoke of God seeing everything, and of Jesus having entered heaven. That is why this verse brings comfort: this Jesus, so great, also understands us. The verses that follow invite us to draw near with confidence.

Today, when you feel weak, tired, or tempted, do not hide from God out of shame. Speak to him honestly, knowing that Jesus understands you and offers you mercy and help in time of need.
exp.8:3:
This passage describes the Most Holy Place. It had a golden censer (some think this refers to the altar of incense). Also there was the ark of the covenant, covered with gold. Inside it was a golden jar with manna, Aaron's rod that budded (put out shoots), and the tables of the law.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He describes the ancient tabernacle to show that Christ brings something better. These objects reminded the people of God's care, his authority, and his law.

For today: remember how God has sustained you, as he did with the manna. And since Christ opened the way to God, you can draw near to him with confidence in prayer.
exp.8:9:
This verse says that the rules of the old system of worship concerned food, drink, and various washings. They were "carnal ordinances," that is, regulations about outward bodily matters.
