"Meats" means food. The word translated "reformation" means renewal or correction: the time when God would set things in their final order.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the tabernacle and its rites pointed toward something greater. They were temporary, until Christ came and fulfilled what they announced.

Today we can remember that no ritual or religious effort cleanses our conscience by itself. If you feel guilty or believe you must earn forgiveness, rest in Christ, whose sacrifice did reach far enough, forever. Obey God, but out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.1:12:
This verse contains two quotations from the Old Testament. Jesús says, "I will put my trust in him," that is, in God. And also: "Behold I and the children which God hath given me." The word "dió" is spelled "dio" today.

The author of Hebrews shows that Jesus became one with us. These phrases are usually related to Isaiah 8:17-18, though some understand them differently. Here Jesus speaks as a man who trusts the Father and presents his own as his family. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers. Then the text explains that he became human to overcome death.

Today we can rest in this: Jesus knows our weakness because he lived it. When you feel alone or afraid, remember that you belong to his family. Trust God as Jesus did, and pray with the assurance that he is with you.
exp.10:32:
This verse speaks of people who, trusting in God, accomplished great things. "Won kingdoms" means they conquered or subdued territories. "Worked righteousness" means they acted uprightly, and "obtained promises" means they saw fulfilled what God had promised. "Stopped the mouths of lions" recalls that God protected some of them from being devoured.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were tired and pressed by suffering. He has just named Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel. Many think "stopped the mouths of lions" alludes to Daniel, though it may also refer to Samson or David. His purpose is to encourage perseverance by showing examples of faith.

Today you can remember that faith is not an abstract idea, but trust that shows itself in brave and upright decisions. Ask God for faith to obey him today in something concrete, even if it frightens you.
exp.9:15:
This verse speaks of a new covenant that God promises. Instead of giving laws written only on stone or in a book, God says he will put them in the heart and write them in the mind or soul of his people. The phrase "after those days" refers to the time that comes after the old covenant. Those who are "sanctified" are the ones God has set apart for himself.

The writer of Hebrews quotes the prophecy of Jeremiah 31:33. He explains that the Holy Spirit bears witness through that Scripture. His purpose is to show that Christ's sacrifice, offered only once, accomplished what the repeated offerings of the temple could not: complete forgiveness and a transformation from within.

For today: do not live your faith only as a list of rules you keep out of obligation. Ask God to shape your desires and your way of thinking himself. Read his Word with confidence, knowing that you are already forgiven and that his Spirit helps you obey with love.
exp.0:1:
This verse says that God, after speaking to his people in many ways in the past, has now spoken to us through his Son. "Last days" means the final times, the last stage of God's plan. "Heir of all things" means that the Son receives everything as his own. And the universe was made through him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. They may have been tempted to return to the old ways. He shows them that Jesus is greater than the prophets and the angels, because he is God's final and complete word.

For today: if you want to know what God is like, look to Jesus. Read about him carefully in the Gospels, and let his voice guide your daily decisions.
exp.10:26:
Moses left Egypt trusting God, and he was not afraid of the anger of the pharaoh. He held on steadily, as though he could see God, even though God is not seen with the eyes. The phrase "him who is invisible" refers to God himself.

The writer of Hebrews recalls the heroes of faith to encourage believers who were under pressure. Some understand this departure to be the exodus with the whole people. Others think it refers to when Moses fled to Midian. The Bible does not make this completely clear, and both views are debated.

When fear of people or of the consequences holds you back, remember that God is present even when you cannot see him. Pray, ask him for courage, and take a step of obedience today, trusting that he sustains you.
exp.9:2:
The explanation says that the sacrifices of the law, repeated every year, actually made sins be remembered. Each time the sacrifice was offered, the people were reminded that their sin was still there and that another sacrifice was needed.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the law was a shadow of the good things to come, not the full reality. If those sacrifices had cleansed completely, they would no longer have had to be repeated. In this way he prepares the way to show that Christ offered a sufficient sacrifice.

Today, if you live with guilt that keeps returning, remember that in Christ there is complete forgiveness. Bring your sin to him honestly, trust in his finished work, and rest in his grace, without trying to earn forgiveness.
exp.8:25:
He says that if Christ's sacrifice had not been enough, he would have had to suffer again and again since the world began. But that was not the case: once, at "the end of the ages" (that is, at the culmination of history), Jesus appeared and offered himself. "Putting away sin" means removing and annulling sin.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He compares Christ with the high priest, who entered the sanctuary every year with blood that was not his own. Christ, by contrast, entered heaven itself with his own sacrifice, made only once.

For today: if Christ has already dealt with sin once for all, you do not have to carry guilt trying to earn forgiveness. Draw near to God with confidence and gratitude, not with fear.
exp.12:21:
It says that the author asks his readers, whom he calls brothers, to receive this message of encouragement and correction with patience. "Suffer" means to bear it with a good attitude, and "word of exhortation" is a message that encourages and also warns. "In few words" means the letter was short and did not go on at length.

The book of Hebrews does not name its author, and we cannot be certain who he was. It speaks to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to give up and turn back. The whole letter shows that Jesus is superior to everything. Here the author closes warmly, asking for openness, right after a blessing and just before mentioning Timothy.

For today: when someone tells you a Bible truth that makes you uncomfortable, do not get defensive right away. Listen with humility, pray, and ask God what he wants to change in you.
exp.11:19:
This verse says that the Israelites could not bear the command God gave at Mount Sinai: even if an animal touched the mountain, it had to be stoned or struck through with an arrow.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who were thinking of returning to their former way of life. He recalls what happened in Exodus 19: God revealed himself with fire, smoke, and a trumpet, and he set limits so that the people would understand his holiness. The contrast is that now believers draw near to God through Christ, not in fear before a forbidden mountain.

For today: come near to God with reverence, but also with confidence. He is holy and deserves respect, and at the same time Jesus opened the way for us to pray without fear of being rejected.
exp.8:4:
This verse describes the upper part of the ark of the covenant. Above it were the cherubims of glory, figures of angelic beings, whose wings covered the mercy seat, that is, the golden lid where the blood was sprinkled for forgiveness. The author says that he cannot now speak in detail about all these things.

The book of Hebrews was written by an author who is not named; tradition has proposed several names, but there is no certainty. It is written to believers with a Jewish background to show them that Christ is greater than the old worship. Here the author goes over the objects of the tabernacle to prepare his explanation: the high priest entered alone only once a year, while Christ opened the way forever.

For today: the mercy seat was the place where God met his people through the blood. Today we can draw near to God with confidence, not because of our merits, but because of Christ. If you feel far from God, pray today and come to him with simplicity.
exp.0:0:
This verse says that God has not stayed silent. Long ago he spoke to our ancestors, the Israelites, the "fathers," through the prophets. He did so at many different times and in many different ways, that is, on various occasions and in varied forms, such as messages, visions, and signs.

Hebrews does not say who wrote it; that is not known for certain. It is addressed to believers with a Jewish background who were tempted to abandon their faith. The author begins by recalling that God spoke in the past, and right away shows that his greatest word came through the Son.

For today: God still wants to communicate with you. Read the Gospels carefully, because there you hear his clearest voice in Jesus.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that when we go through correction or discipline, God treats us as his children. The word "endure" in the verse is an older form of the verb "endure," and "chastening" here means discipline or training rather than punishment for its own sake. The closing question is clear: no father who truly cares for his son stops correcting him.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers worn down by trials and encourages them by citing Proverbs 3:11-12. He reminds them that difficulties can be part of God's care. Not all suffering comes from correction for sin; the text speaks of the discipline that shapes character.

For today: when you go through a hard situation, instead of asking only "why me?", ask "what is God wanting to teach me?". Pray with humility, trust that He loves you, and let that trial draw you closer to Him rather than push you away.
exp.12:2:
It says we should remember those in prison, that is, keep them present in our hearts and in prayer, as if we ourselves were imprisoned with them. The same goes for those who are mistreated and suffering: we should remember them because we too have a body and can suffer. The phrase about the body speaks of our human condition, and perhaps also of the body of Christ.

The author of Hebrews does not identify himself; we do not know for certain who he was. He writes to Christians who had endured imprisonment and losses for their faith. Here he gives concrete instructions on how to live out brotherly love: hospitality, solidarity with those who suffer, faithfulness in marriage, and trust in God.

Today we can choose a person who is suffering, such as a prisoner, a sick person, or a brother or sister persecuted for their faith, pray for them by name, and look for a simple way to help them: a visit, a letter, or an offering.
exp.12:6:
This verse asks us to remember the leaders who taught us the word of God. The words "have the rule over you" point to those who guide and lead the community. It also invites us to follow their faith, paying attention to how their way of life ended up.

The letter to the Hebrews does not say with certainty who wrote it. It is addressed to believers of Jewish background who faced pressure and temptations to turn back. Earlier, the author encouraged them to live without greed and to trust that God never abandons them. Later, he reminds them that Jesus Christ does not change, and so they should not be carried away by strange teachings.

Today we can thank those who taught us the faith, perhaps a pastor, a grandmother, or a teacher. Think of one person whose life was faithful to God, and imitate one concrete virtue of theirs this week.
exp.5:14:
The explanation says that Abraham waited patiently and so received what God had promised him. The phrase "steadfast endurance" is an old expression meaning patience, staying power, not giving up while waiting. The phrase "obtained the promise" means that he received the fulfillment of what God had told him.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who were tired and tempted to abandon their faith. He gives them the example of Abraham, to whom God promised blessing and many descendants, and confirmed it with an oath. Abraham saw the beginning of the fulfillment, especially with the birth of Isaac, though the full promise reaches beyond his lifetime. Some scholars emphasize this last point; the text itself does not detail it here.

When God has given you a promise and the answer is slow in coming, do not let it go. Keep trusting, praying, and obeying, because patience rests on the fact that God is faithful.
exp.3:4:
This verse repeats a phrase from Psalm 95: "They shall not enter into my rest." The author of Hebrews quotes it again to remind his readers that God spoke these words in earnest, as a warning. The word "rest" means peace and settled trust in God, a place where a person stops struggling on their own.

The author writes to believers who were in danger of growing weary or drifting away from the faith. He reminds them of what happened to the people of Israel in the wilderness: God offered them rest in the promised land, but many did not enter because of their disobedience and lack of trust. The author shows that this promise of rest remains open to those who believe.

Today we can ask ourselves where it is hard for us to trust God. Instead of hardening our hearts, we can obey his voice with simplicity and hand over our burdens, knowing that he invites us to rest in him.
exp.9:32:
It says that the believers being written to were publicly exposed to insults and suffering, like someone placed on a stage for everyone to see. "Insults" are mockery and offense; "hardships" are severe trials. It also says they became companions of others who were going through the same things, meaning they did not stay apart from them.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were under pressure because of their faith and were tempted to give up. He asks them to remember the early days after they came to know Christ. He reminds them of their earlier steadfastness to encourage them not to lose their confidence.

For today: when someone suffers for their faith or through a trial, do not leave them alone. Standing with them through visits, prayer, or concrete help is a real way of loving, and it also strengthens your own trust in God.
exp.10:39:
He says that God had prepared something better for us, the believers who live after Christ. For this reason the faithful of the Old Testament did not reach their fullness "without us." "Perfected" means brought to their goal or fulfillment. All of them will be made complete together.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were suffering and could be tempted to abandon the faith. He has just recalled heroes who trusted God even though they endured hardship and did not see the promise fulfilled. Many understand that "something better" refers to Christ and his finished work, although the text does not spell this out.

Today, this reminds you that you do not walk alone. Your faith is part of a great story, with believers from every age. If you are slow to see answers, keep trusting: God works through a plan that includes all of his people.
exp.4:1:
The explanation says that the high priest can deal patiently and tenderly with those who do not know and with those who stray from the path, because he himself is surrounded by weakness. The word translated here as "high priest" is the one the verse itself uses in its context, and the phrase "can have compassion" here speaks of dealing gently, without harshness.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, explains how the priesthood of Israel worked. The priest was a man chosen from among the people, which is why he knew human weakness from the inside. The author is preparing the way to show that Jesus is an even better high priest, who also understands us.

When someone fails or does not understand something, remember your own weaknesses and treat them with patience, not with pride. And if you have failed, draw near to God with confidence: He understands and is merciful.
exp.11:22:
This verse continues to describe where believers in Christ have come. It speaks of "the general assembly and church of the firstborn," that is, the family of God's children who have an inheritance and a special place, whose names are "written" in heaven, meaning recorded there. It also mentions God as the Judge of all, and "the spirits of just men made perfect," which many understand to be God's faithful people already made complete by Christ.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to Jewish Christians who were tempted to turn back because of their trials. He compares Mount Sinai, full of terror, with Mount Zion, where God receives us by grace. Some interpret "firstborn" as the whole church; others understand it as believers already in heaven.

For today: if your name is written in heaven, do not live in fear or alone. You belong to a great family. Pray and serve with that assurance, trusting that Christ has made you acceptable before God.
exp.10:24:
Moses made a decision: he chose to suffer together with the people of God rather than to enjoy the pleasures of a comfortable life that involved sin. "Suffer affliction" means to be mistreated or to undergo hardship. "Pleasures of sin for a season" refers to pleasures that last only a short time. Moses saw that those pleasures were not worth the cost.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who faced pressure and suffering. He gives them examples of people of faith. Moses grew up in Pharaoh's palace, but he chose to identify with Israel, an enslaved people. The text says he did this by faith, trusting in the reward that God would give.

Today, obeying God sometimes costs us acceptance, advantages, or peace of mind. Before deciding, ask yourself: "Does this give me only a passing relief, or does it keep me faithful to God?" Trusting Him can help you choose what lasts.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that Jesus, the Son of God, shows the glory of the Father like a light and is the exact image of what God is. The "brightness" is the radiance that comes out from a light, and the "express image" is the very being at the core of who God is. Jesús also holds up everything that has been created by his powerful word. Being the one who "purged" our sins means that he himself cleansed us from our sins. Then he "sat down" at the place of honor and authority beside God, here called "the Majesty on high."

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He shows them that God no longer spoke only through the prophets, but through his Son, who is greater than the prophets and the angels.

For today: if Jesus holds up all things and has already cleansed your sin, you can rest in him. When you feel guilty or afraid, trust in his finished work and in his constant care.
exp.6:6:
It says that, beyond all dispute, the one who blesses is greater than the one who is blessed. "Dispute" here means argument or doubt. The lesser is the one in the lower place, and the greater is the one who holds the higher position.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show that Melchizedek is greater than Abraham, because Melchizedek blessed him and received tithes from him. So the priesthood of Melchizedek, which points to Christ, is greater than the Levitical priesthood.

Today we can remember that Jesus is greater than every tradition, ritual, or religious leader. Before trusting in anything to feel accepted by God, return to Christ, our great high priest, and rest in his complete work.
exp.10:35:
This verse speaks of believers who suffered mockery and beatings. "Insults" are public humiliations and abuse; "lashings" are punishments with a whip. In addition, some were chained and locked up in prison, that is, deprived of their freedom because of their faith.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and whose identity has been much debated, writes to Christians of Jewish background who faced pressure and temptation to abandon Christ. In chapter 11 he reviews the heroes of faith. Earlier he showed those who prevailed with visible victories; now he shows those who also trusted God but suffered. In this way he reminds them that faith does not always bring immediate relief.

Today we can remember that suffering does not mean God has abandoned us or that our faith is weak. If you are mocked or mistreated for following Christ, stand firm, and pray for those who go through persecution.
exp.5:1:
This verse continues a list of basic teachings of the Christian faith: the baptisms (in the plural), the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. Laying on of hands means placing hands on someone, a gesture that in the Bible was used to bless, to pray for a person, or to set someone apart for a service. It is not known with certainty which baptisms are meant; some think of different kinds of washing or purification, or of Christian baptism compared with other washings.

The author of Hebrews (we do not know for certain who he was) writes to believers who had stopped growing. He tells them that they already have the foundations and that it is time to grow into maturity, without starting over from the beginning.

For today: do not settle for the basics of your faith. Be thankful for the foundations, but keep learning, reading the Bible, and putting into practice what you understand, so that you grow every day.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that God did not place the angels as rulers over the world to come, meaning the new age that God will bring and that the letter is talking about. The explanation's note on the word "subjected" is not needed here, since that word does not appear in the King James wording, and the note on the earlier word for "salvation" is likewise set aside because it does not match any word in this verse.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself and whom we cannot identify with certainty, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to let their faith grow weak. He has already shown that Jesus is greater than the angels. Now he makes clear that the future kingdom will not be handed over to them. Right after this, he quotes Psalm 8, which speaks of the human being crowned with glory, and he will apply it to Jesus.

For today: do not place your final trust in anything created, not even in impressive spiritual things. Fix your gaze on Jesus, who holds authority and invites you to persevere with firmness in your salvation.
exp.6:26:
This verse says that Jesus, our high priest, does not need to offer sacrifices every day as the other priests did. They first offered for their own sins and then for the sins of the people. Jesus, by contrast, did it once, when he offered himself.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Christ is superior to the priests of the law. Those priests were weak and sinful men; Jesus is holy, without sin, and his sacrifice is complete and does not need to be repeated.

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through effort or carry guilt that has already been forgiven. You can draw near to God with confidence, because Jesus has already paid for everything. Rest in his finished work and respond with gratitude and obedience.
exp.10:17:
This verse explains why Abraham's test was so hard. God had told him: "In Isaac shall your offspring be called." The word "offspring" means descendants, that is, the children and future generations. God's promise depended on Isaac.

The writer of Hebrews is speaking to believers who needed to persevere, and he sets Abraham before them as an example of faith. He quotes Genesis 21:12. Abraham received a promise and then a command that seemed to contradict it: to offer Isaac. The verses that follow say that Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead. In this way he trusted God, even without understanding how God would keep his word.

For today: when what God says seems not to fit with the life you are living, do not abandon your trust. Remember that God is faithful and can act where you see no way out. Keep obeying with humility and peace.
exp.7:8:
This verse says that the new covenant would not be like the one God made with Israel when he brought them out of Egypt. God remembers that moment with tenderness: he took them by the hand, like a small child. But the people did not remain; that is, they were not faithful. The phrase "I regarded them not" means that God stopped caring for them as a people under that covenant; some understand it as God turning away from them with sorrow.

The author of Hebrews quotes the prophet Jeremiah (31:31-34). He writes to believers of Jewish background to show them that Jesus brings a better covenant, because the old one depended on human faithfulness, and that faithfulness failed.

For today: let us not trust in our own steadfastness, but in the work of Christ. God holds us by the hand, and through his grace he changes our hearts from within.
exp.2:12:
It says that believers should encourage and warn one another every day, for as long as it can still be called "today." The purpose is that none of them be hardened, that is, that none become numb to God, deceived by sin. The verb rendered here as "exhort" means to encourage, advise, and urge. The word "but" is not needed in this verse; the sentence simply continues the thought.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to Jewish Christians who were tempted to turn away from Christ. He quotes Psalm 95 and reminds his readers of the people of Israel in the wilderness, who did not trust God and did not enter his rest. He warns them that unbelief begins gradually.

For today: seek out a brother or sister in the faith and this week encourage them with a word or a message, and pray with them. Also allow someone you trust to speak to you honestly.
exp.12:23:
He says the readers should greet all their leaders, that is, those who guide and care for them, and also all the saints, that is, all the believers. Then he adds that the Christians of Italy send their greetings to them. The Greek-based wording, in which the greeting is addressed to "all," is rendered in the verse you have as "salute all them that have the rule over you." As for the word "saints," it does not refer to people who are perfect, but to those who belong to God.

The author of Hebrews closes his letter with farewells. We do not know for certain who wrote it, and this has been much debated. The phrase "They of Italy" may mean that he is writing from Italy, or that he is sending greetings from Italians who are with him, and not everyone agrees. With this he shows closeness to his readers, whom he had earlier urged to persevere.

Today we can value those who care for us spiritually. This week, greet or write a few words of thanks to your pastor or some leader, and also to a brother who may feel lonely. A simple greeting strengthens unity.
exp.6:4:
This verse says that the priests descended from Levi had a command in the law of Moses: to collect tithes from the people of Israel. In other words, they took a tenth from their own brothers, who were also descendants of Abraham.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus, a priest after the manner of Melchizedek, is superior to the Levitical priesthood. First he points out that the Levites collected tithes by command of the law. Later he will say that Abraham gave tithes to Melchizedek, which shows the greatness of Melchizedek.

For today: value Jesus as your supreme priest. Instead of trusting in rituals or traditions, draw near to God with confidence through Christ, and pray each day knowing that he intercedes for you.
exp.1:13:
It says that the "children," that is, the believers, are human beings of flesh and blood. For this reason Jesus also became human, truly and completely. He did this so that through his death he might destroy the devil, who held the power of death, meaning authority over it. The word "destroy" can be understood as to take away its strength or to render it powerless.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know with certainty, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He has just quoted Old Testament passages where Christ calls his people his "brothers." Now he explains why Jesus had to share our humanity: to rescue us from within our very condition.

For today: if you fear death, suffering, or the future, remember that Jesus went through these things and overcame them. He understands you and is with you. You can pray with confidence and live with hope.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that whoever enters God's rest stops working to earn his favor, just as God rested from his work when creation was finished. "Rest" here means peace, freedom from striving, and security in what God has already done. "Works" here refers to human efforts to deserve salvation.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to give up or turn back. He reminds them that Joshua led the people into the land, but not into the final rest. That rest is still open, and so he urges them not to harden their hearts like the generation in the wilderness.

For today: if you are tired from trying to be good enough before God, trust in what Christ has already done. Rest in his grace, and from there serve him with gratitude, not with fear.
exp.8:18:
Here the author recalls that Moses read to the people all the commandments of the law. Then he took the blood of calves and male goats, mixed it with water, and used red wool and hyssop, a small plant used for sprinkling. With these he sprinkled the book of the law and all the people.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the first covenant, made at Sinai (Exodus 24), was sealed with blood. In this way he prepares his argument: if that covenant required blood, the new covenant is confirmed with the blood of Christ.

For today: God draws near to us through a serious covenant, confirmed with blood. This reminds us that his forgiveness cost a great deal. We can receive it with gratitude and respond with sincere obedience, not out of fear, but out of love.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that it was necessary for the copies of the things in the heavens, that is, the tabernacle and its objects, to be purified with the blood of animals. But the heavenly realities themselves needed something better: far better sacrifices. The word for the copies is one that the verse above renders as "patterns," and the word for the heavenly things is the one rendered "heavenly things." The verse's word "therefore" marks the conclusion drawn from what has just been said. The plural "sacrifices" probably points to the excellence of Christ's one sacrifice.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the tabernacle system was a shadow, and that Christ is the reality. For this reason he compares the ancient blood with his own.

For today: you do not have to achieve your cleansing through effort or rituals. You can draw near to God with confidence, resting in what Christ has already done for you, and live with gratitude and simplicity.
exp.0:10:
It says that heaven and earth, although they seem firm, will not last forever. They will wear out like old clothing. By contrast, the Lord "remains the same," that is, he does not change or come to an end. The phrase "they shall perish" means that they will cease to exist as we know them, and "shall wax old" means that they will wear out over time.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 102:25-27 to show that the Son is superior to the angels. Here the text speaks of the Son as Lord and Creator, since it calls him the one who laid the foundation of the earth. The angels are servants, but the Son is eternal. Some explain that creation will be renewed rather than simply destroyed; the text does not give further details.

Today we can let go of anxiety about things that wear out: money, health, plans. All of that is valuable, but it is not the most secure thing. Place your hope in Christ, who remains the same.
exp.8:26:
It says that every human being is appointed to die only once, and that after death comes God's judgment. The phrase "is appointed" means that God has so arranged it. "Unto men" means all people, not only males.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He compares the single death of people with the single sacrifice of Christ. The priests offered blood every year, but Jesus offered himself once. In this way, the verse prepares the message that Christ takes away sin and will come again to save those who are waiting for him.

For today: since life is brief and does not repeat, live it with humility and gratitude. Instead of fearing judgment, trust in Christ, who has already borne your sins, and seek today to be reconciled with God and with others.
exp.6:8:
This verse says that Levi, the ancestor of the Jewish priests, "payed" tithes to Melchizedek when Abraham paid them. "Payed" is the old form of "paid," and "as I may so say" means it is a way of putting it. Levi had not yet been born, but he was, so to speak, within his great-grandfather Abraham.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named and whose identity is debated, writes to Christians of Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus, a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, is greater than the Levitical priesthood. If the very priests descended from Levi honored Melchizedek through Abraham, then Melchizedek's priesthood is greater.

For today: do not place your trust in inherited traditions or achievements. Jesus is our perfect high priest, and through Him we can draw near to God with full confidence.
exp.4:10:
It says that the author has much to explain about Christ as priest according to the order of Melchizedek, but that it is hard to put into words. The reason is not that the subject is bad, but that the readers are "dull of hearing," that is, slow or lazy to understand and listen.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers who had been in the faith for a long time, but had become stuck. He has just mentioned Melchizedek and wants to go deeper, but he pauses to correct them kindly. He reminds them that they should already be teaching others, and not need to have the basics repeated to them.

For today: ask yourself whether you are growing in your faith or just repeating what you have always done. Set aside time regularly to read the Bible carefully and to ask God for a heart willing to learn deeper things.
exp.10:11:
From one man, Abraham, who was already as good as dead (that is, nearly dead, without the strength to have children because of his age), came a descendant as great as the stars of the sky and as the sand on the seashore, too many to count. "On the seashore" is simply the beach.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who needed to persevere. He gives them examples of faith from the Old Testament. Here he recalls that Abraham and Sara trusted that God would fulfill his promise, even though humanly it seemed impossible (Genesis 15:5; 22:17).

For today: when a situation seems closed or without a way out, do not look only at your limitations. God is faithful and can do something great out of something small. Trust in Him, take the next step you know how to take, and wait with patience.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that Moses was faithful in all that God entrusted to him, as a servant within the house of God. Here the verse's own wording stands in for the source phrases: the reader should understand "truly" as the verse's "verily," and "was" as its "was." His service helped bear witness, that is, to announce ahead of time, what God would say later.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to Christians from a Jewish background who faced pressure and temptation to abandon the faith. He honors Moses, but shows that Jesus is greater: Moses was a servant in the house, and Christ is the Son over it. Many understand that what Moses announced pointed toward Christ.

For today: faithfulness in what God entrusts to us has value, even when our role seems small. Serve with constancy, and keep your trust placed in Christ, who is greater than all.
exp.12:14:
It says that, through Jesus, believers are to offer God a sacrifice of praise at all times. That sacrifice is "the fruit of our lips," meaning words that acknowledge and honor God's name. The old form of a word used in the verse is rewritten here as nothing more than the plain "to" used in the verse, and "confess" here means openly declaring, giving thanks, and proclaiming.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were suffering rejection and pressure. He reminds them that Jesus suffered outside the gate and that they do not have a permanent city here. Since they no longer offer the sacrifices of the temple, he tells them that their offering now is praise, together with doing good.

Today, even in difficult days, we can speak aloud a sincere gratitude to God: when we wake up, at work, or in the family. Praising does not depend on how we feel, but on who God is.
exp.9:1:
It says that if the sacrifices of the law had truly been able to cleanse, they would have stopped being offered. Those who worshipped, once they were completely cleansed, would no longer feel guilty. The phrase about those who offer this worship means "those who offer this worship"; the inner weight of guilt is what is meant by the consciousness of sin.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, is writing to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that the sacrifices repeated each year were only a shadow, pointing to something greater. That they had to be repeated was a sign that they did not remove sin completely. This prepares the argument that Christ's sacrifice does, once and for all.

Today: if you have trusted in Christ, do not carry a guilt that he has already carried. When you remember a sin, confess it honestly, but rest in his complete forgiveness, and live with gratitude rather than fear.
exp.10:2:
Through faith, it says, we understand that the universe was formed by the word of God. "The worlds" refers to the world and to time, that is, to everything that was created. "Framed" means put in order or prepared. What we see did not come from anything visible, but from the word of God, which could not be seen.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who needed to persevere. After defining faith, he begins a list of witnesses from the past. First he mentions creation, something no one witnessed, which is accepted by trusting God. Then come Abel, Enoch, and others.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that the God who created everything by his word is still at work even when you cannot see it. Trust him today in a specific situation.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that Christ has already come as high priest of the good things that God promised. He serves in a greater and more perfect tabernacle, one not built by human hands, that is, not part of this created world. "That is to say" means "in other words."

The author of Hebrews was writing to Christians with a Jewish background who were tempted to return to the old rituals. He shows them that those ceremonies, with their foods, washings and sacrifices, could not cleanse the conscience. They were a sign pointing toward something better. With Christ came the time of reformation, or renewal. Scholars explain in various ways exactly what that tabernacle is, but they all agree that it refers to heaven, where Christ serves.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus has already completed the work. We do not need to carry guilt or earn forgiveness through religious effort; we can draw near to God with confidence.
exp.6:25:
This verse says that Jesus is the high priest we truly needed. The word "high priest" is used in the verse itself. He is described as holy, meaning completely devoted to God; harmless, without malice; and undefiled, without any stain. He is "separate from sinners," which does not mean that he looked down on them, but that he is different from them because he has no sin. And he was "made higher than the heavens," meaning he was exalted to a supreme place.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is superior to the priests of the old covenant, who were weak and needed to offer sacrifices for their own sins.

For today: because Jesus is perfect and lives interceding for us, we can approach God with confidence, without fear, even after we have failed.
exp.7:4:
They say that the priests of the temple on earth served in something that was only a "shadow and copy," that is, a sketch or reflection of the realities of heaven. God told Moses to build the tabernacle exactly according to the pattern he had shown him on the mountain.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is a superior High Priest. The worship of the tabernacle was good, but it pointed to something greater, and that greater thing is fulfilled in Christ and in his heavenly ministry.

For today: do not cling to what is only a sign or shadow, such as rituals or customs, and neglect Christ, who is the reality. Let your faith rest in him and not only in outward forms.
exp.6:2:
The explanation says that Melchizedek appears in Scripture with no mention of father, mother, or genealogy, and with no record of his birth or his death. The words "ancestry" and "like" are used in the passage to mean family line and resemblance. In the account, Melchizedek therefore serves as a picture of the Son of God, whose priesthood never ends.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to return to the old ways. He uses the silence of Genesis 14 about Melchizedek to show that Christ's priesthood is greater than that of Levi. Some understand that Melchizedek was a real man described with this purpose in view; others understand him to be a special appearance of Christ. The Bible does not fully settle the matter.

Today you can rest in the fact that Jesus is your permanent priest. His care for you does not depend on taking turns and does not come to an end, so you can approach God with confidence at any time.
exp.4:9:
He says that God himself appointed Jesus as high priest, and that his priesthood follows the order of Melchisedec. This means that he does not belong to the line of priests descended from Aaron, but to a different kind of priesthood, one that is unique and older.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers who had stopped growing in their spiritual life. He has just said that Jesus learned obedience through suffering. Now he mentions Melchisedec, a king and priest who appears in Genesis 14, and says there is much to explain, but his readers have become slow to understand.

For today: if Jesus is our high priest appointed by God, we can draw near to him with confidence in prayer. And it is worth asking ourselves whether we are still growing, or whether we are still content with milk when God wants to give us solid food.
exp.9:35:
It says we need patience, meaning steady endurance, to keep doing what God wants and so receive what He has promised. The phrase "is necessary for you" means "they need it." "Receive" is what the verse says in place of the word for obtaining. Patience is not standing still, but persevering in obeying God while the promise arrives.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to believers who had already suffered: some were imprisoned, and others lost their possessions. Now they were at risk of growing tired and giving up. So he reminds them of their earlier faith, speaks to them of a better inheritance in heaven, and encourages them not to let go of their confidence, for the coming of the Lord will not be delayed.

For today: when obeying God costs you something or the answer takes a long time, do not give up. Choose one concrete step of faithfulness today, such as praying, forgiving, or serving, and trust that God fulfills what He promises.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that Scripture bears witness about Jesus: he is a priest forever, not for a limited time. The phrase "after the order of Melchisedec" means that his priesthood is of the same kind as Melchisedec's, and different from the priesthood of Levi. Here, the word "testifieth" means that the Bible affirms it.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, quotes Psalm 110:4 to show his readers, Christians of Jewish background, that Jesus is a priest by the power of an endless life, that is, a life that does not come to an end. For this reason his priesthood replaces the one under the law, which was weak.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus intercedes for us without growing weary or coming to an end. When you fail or feel that God is far away, come near with confidence in prayer, knowing that your priest lives forever.
exp.12:4:
This verse asks that our way of living not be marked by covetousness, that is, by the desire to always have more money and things. Instead, we should be content with what we have now. The reason is a promise from God: "I will never leave you, nor forsake you," which means that he will never abandon us or let us go.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers who had suffered pressure and losses because of their faith. Shortly before, he speaks of love for one another, of caring for prisoners, and of purity in marriage. Here he adds the subject of money, and he supports his advice with an ancient promise that God gave to his people in the Old Testament.

Today, before buying something on impulse or envying what belongs to others, we can stop and give thanks for what we already have, remembering that our security is in God.
exp.12:15:
This verse calls us not to forget to do good and to share what we have with others. Here "sharing" means giving, being generous and standing with others, especially those in need, rather than simply chatting. It says that God is pleased with such offerings, that is, with gifts made out of ordinary daily life.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who live under pressure. He has just spoken of the sacrifice of praise, and now he adds that worship is also shown through deeds. Since we do not have a lasting city here, we can live with open hands.

Today, you could look this week for someone with a specific need, a neighbor, a relative, or someone in your church, and help them with your time, your food, or your money. Do it as worship to God.
exp.6:12:
He of whom these things are spoken, Jesus, the one Psalm 110 speaks about, belongs to a tribe other than the priestly one. The phrase "served at the altar" means that he served as priest at the altar. No member of the tribe of Judah had served there, because the law reserved that office for the tribe of Levi, and especially for the descendants of Aaron.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is a superior priest. If the priesthood changed, the law that governed it changed as well. Jesus came from Judah, and so his priesthood is not based on family inheritance but on the order of Melchizedek.

For today: you do not need merit, lineage, or rituals to come near to God. Jesus, our priest, opens the way for you. Go to him with confidence in prayer.
exp.8:6:
Hebrews 9:7 says that only the high priest entered the second place, the Most Holy Place, and he did so only once a year. He never went in without blood. He offered it first for his own sins and then for the sins of the people committed in ignorance, that is, sins committed without their realizing it or without evil intent.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, describes the Old Testament tabernacle. This refers to the Day of Atonement, according to Leviticus 16. He wants to show believers with a Jewish background that this system had limits: access to God was restricted and had to be repeated every year.

For today: God does not take sin lightly, but He also does not keep us far away. You can approach Him with gratitude and confidence, remembering that Christ opened the way with his own blood.
exp.3:10:
He says we should make an effort, put in diligence, to enter God's rest. "Let us labour" is the phrase in the verse itself, so no separate explanation is needed here. He also warns that no one should fall by the same example of disobedience, that is, that no one should repeat the mistake of not believing and not obeying God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who could grow weary or turn back. He reminds them of the people of Israel in the wilderness, who did not enter the rest promised to them because of their unbelief. He then adds that the Word of God reveals what is in the heart.

Today, trusting God requires a daily decision. When you feel tired or tempted to rely only on yourself, pause, pray, and obey what God has already shown you in his Word.
exp.11:0:
This verse says we are surrounded by a great crowd of witnesses, that is, people of faith from the past. For this reason, we should set aside everything that slows us down, above all the sin that tangles us up, and run with endurance, that is, with perseverance, the race that God has set before us.

The author of Hebrews is not known for certain. He writes to Christians who are tired and tempted to give up. Just before, chapter 11 recalls men and women who trusted in God, and these are the witnesses. Many understand that they do not watch us from the stands, but that their example testifies that it is worth trusting in God.

Today you might ask yourself: what habit, burden, or sin is holding me back in my life with God? Ask Him for help to let it go, and keep moving forward with steadiness, looking to Jesus, not to your own strength.
exp.5:8:
He says that the author is confident that his readers, whom he calls "beloved," are in a better situation than those who fall away. "Better things" are good things that accompany salvation, and the sentence "though we thus speak" means: "even though I have just spoken to you with such harsh words."

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, has just issued a very serious warning about turning away from the faith. With the image of the land that bears fruit and the land full of thorns, he now softens his tone. He wants to shake them out of indifference, not discourage them. He sees real fruit in them: their service and their love for the saints.

For today: God's warnings are not meant to crush us, but to wake us up. Examine what fruits of love and service are in your life, and encourage someone in your church with words of trust and hope.
exp.8:7:
The Holy Spirit was showing something by the way the ancient tabernacle worked. While the first tabernacle (the outer part, where the priests went in) was still standing, the way into the most holy place (where God's presence was) had not yet been opened. Here "manifest" means made known or opened.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background. He explains that the rituals of the tabernacle pointed to something greater. Only the high priest entered the most holy place, once a year, and with blood. That showed that access to God was still limited.

For today: in Christ, the way is open. You can come near to God with confidence, not depending on rituals or go-betweens, but trusting in what Jesus has done for you.
exp.11:21:
This verse says that believers in Christ are no longer standing before a terrifying mountain, as Israel did at Sinai, but have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God. There is the heavenly Jerusalem and an assembly of thousands of angels. "Come unto" means that they have drawn near. "Company" means a gathering or a multitude.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to abandon their faith. He compares the fear of Sinai, where even Moses trembled, with the privilege of drawing near to God through Jesus. Many understand the heavenly city to be the spiritual reality to which we already have access.

For today: when you feel that God is distant or that your faith is small, remember that Christ opened the way for you. Pray with reverence, but with confidence, because you have been invited into his presence.
exp.12:5:
This verse says that, because of God's promise, we can speak with assurance and without fear. The word "boldly" means with confidence, without doubting. A "helper" is someone who assists us and holds us up. We say that the Lord is our help and that we do not have to fear what any person may do to us.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were facing pressure. He has just reminded them of the promise, "I will never leave you, nor forsake you." So he says "so that": since God promises to be with them, they can answer with courage. The quotation at the end is from Psalm 118:6.

When you feel afraid of rejection, a threat, or what others think of you, repeat this truth in prayer: "The Lord is my helper." Then take the right step in front of you, trusting that God goes with you.
exp.5:6:
It says that the earth which soaks up the rain that falls on it many times, and which yields a good crop for those who work it, receives God's blessing.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers who were at risk of drifting away from the faith. Earlier he spoke of those who tasted God's blessings and then let them go. Now he uses the picture of a field: the same rain falls on all the ground, but the result is different. Those who interpret this passage disagree about the fate of those who fall away, but all agree that it is a serious warning.

Today, it is not enough to hear the Word many times. God looks for fruit: love, obedience, and perseverance. Ask yourself what you have done with what you have already received, and take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.4:12:
It says that whoever still lives on "milk," that is, on the most basic teachings, is not skilled in "the word of righteousness," meaning the teaching about what is right and pleasing to God. The reason is that such a person is a babe in the faith. "Unskilful" means lacking experience or ability. "Partaker" means one who feeds on that.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, gently rebukes believers who had already been in the faith for some time but had not matured. They should have been teaching others, and they still needed to review the basics. He speaks to them about Christ as priest and wants to lead them to a firmer faith.

For today: do not settle for the basics. Devote steady time to reading the Bible, studying it, and putting it into practice, so that your faith grows and you can help others.
exp.9:8:
This verse says that Christ, when he came into the world, presented himself before God with complete willingness: "I come to do your will." With that, he "takes away the first," that is, he sets aside the animal sacrifices of the law, "so that he may establish the second," that is, the last: God's will carried out in Christ.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 40 and applies it to Jesus. He writes to believers of Jewish background who valued the temple sacrifices very highly. He wants to show them that those sacrifices pointed to something greater and could not remove sin completely. Jesus, through his obedience and the offering of his body, opened a new and final way.

For today: we do not have to earn forgiveness through religious effort. Rest in what Christ has already done, and respond as he did, saying to God each day: "Here I am, let your will be done."
exp.10:14:
The explanation says that if those believers had kept thinking fondly about the land they came out of, they would have had many chances to go back. The phrase "they really had the time" means they truly had the opportunity. But they did not return.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, speaks of Abraham, Sarah, and other patriarchs. He wants to encourage weary believers to stay firm. These men and women lived as strangers, and their eyes were fixed on what God had promised them, not on what they had left behind. That is why, the text says, God is not ashamed to be called their God.

For today: when following God becomes hard, do not keep looking back wistfully at what you left. Ask him to fix your heart on his promises, and take one concrete step of faithfulness today, even if you do not yet see the result.
exp.1:6:
It says that God made human beings a little lower than the angels, yet He honored them in a special way. The words "Thou crownedst him" in the verse express the same idea, and "didst set him over" carries the sense of putting him in charge. In other words, God gave humanity dignity and entrusted it with caring for what He created.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 8, written by David. He wants to show that the world to come is not placed under the angels, but under human beings. Yet we do not yet see everything subject to humanity. That is why he points to Jesus: being a man, He was made lower for a time, suffered death for everyone, and was crowned with glory. Many understand the text to speak of humanity and of Jesus as its head.

For today: your life has a worth that God Himself gave. When you feel small or unimportant, remember that God sees you, honors you, and has entrusted you with responsibilities. Take care of them with gratitude.
exp.3:15:
The explanation says that we should draw near to God with confidence, without fear. The verse's words "come boldly" mean "draw near," that is, approach. "The throne of grace" is the place where God reigns and offers his undeserved favor. There we receive mercy (forgiveness and compassion) and find grace, that is, help that comes right when we most need it, at the time of need.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to believers who are weary and tempted to give up. He reminds them that Jesus, called the high priest, went through trials as we do, yet without sinning. For that reason he understands our weaknesses. Since he is with the Father, we can draw near with assurance.

Today, when you feel weak, guilty, or pressured, do not wait to get yourself together first. Pray sincerely and tell God what you are facing. He receives you with mercy and gives you help in your time of need.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that the Holy Spirit speaks through the Scriptures. The words "if you will hear" are an older way of saying "if you hear" or "if you listen." The word "today" stresses that God's voice is heard now, not only in the past.

The author of Hebrews has just said that Christ is greater than Moses and that we are his house if we hold firmly to our confidence. Now he quotes Psalm 95 and attributes it to the Holy Spirit. He does this as a warning: the people of Israel in the wilderness heard God, but they hardened their hearts. The sentence continues in the next verse.

For today: do not leave obedience for tomorrow. When you sense that God is speaking to you through his Word, respond today with a concrete step: forgiving, praying, correcting something, or trusting in him.
exp.8:23:
This verse says that Christ did not enter a temple built by human hands, which was only a copy or shadow of the true one. He entered heaven itself, to appear now before God on our behalf. The holy place where God was worshiped is the sanctuary, and the copy or shadow is what the temple was.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the temple's system of sacrifices pointed to something greater. The high priest entered the most holy place each year with blood that was not his own, but Jesus entered with his own sacrifice, once and for all.

Today you can rest knowing that Jesus is before God for you right now. You do not have to earn access to God through effort or rituals. When you feel guilty or far from God, pray with confidence, remembering that Christ has already opened the way and represents you.
exp.9:20:
This verse says that believers have a "great priest" over the "house of God." A priest was the one who presented the people before God. Here Jesus is spoken of as that superior priest. The "house of God" refers to his people, the family of those who believe in him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and whom we cannot identify with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to abandon their faith. Earlier he spoke of Jesus' single sacrifice. Now he summarizes: thanks to him we can draw near to God with boldness, and this prepares the invitation that follows: let us draw near with a sincere heart in faith.

For today: when you feel unworthy or far from God, remember that Jesus is already interceding for you. Pray with confidence, without fear, because you do not go alone; you have someone who represents you and receives you.
exp.1:17:
It says that Jesus suffered when he was tempted, and that is why he can help those who are going through temptation today. The word translated "suffered" means endured pain or hardship; "help" here means to come to someone's aid; and "high priest" refers to the chief priest.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the letter does not mention, writes to believers from a Jewish background who needed encouragement not to abandon their faith. Earlier he explains that Jesus became human, sharing in our flesh and blood, so that he could be a merciful and faithful high priest. This verse completes that thought: Jesus understands our struggle because he lived through it.

For today: when you face temptation, do not hide or feel ashamed. Bring your weakness to Jesus in prayer, with confidence, knowing that he does not look on you with indifference but understands you and wants to help you.
exp.2:5:
He says that Christ rules God's house as a Son, not as a servant. That house is us, that is, God's people, on one condition: that we hold firm to the end the confidence and joyful hope we have. The explanation of the old phrase "until the end" is simply "until the end," and "to hold fast" is the same as "to keep." The "rejoicing of the hope" refers to the hope in which we can rejoice.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background who felt tempted to abandon their faith under pressure. He compares Moses, faithful as a servant, with Christ, faithful as a Son. Then, using the example of the wilderness, he encourages them not to harden their hearts.

For today: when tiredness or doubt comes, do not trust in your own strength. Seek Christ in prayer, in the Bible, and in the company of other believers, so that you may stay firm in the hope.
exp.11:12:
It says we should walk on straight paths, with firm and well-directed steps. The explanation notes that one word means straight, and that a person who is "lame" is someone who walks hurt or weak. The idea is that the weak one should not be pushed off the path, but healed.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers worn down by suffering and by God's discipline. We do not know for certain who the author was. He encourages them, and asks that the way they walk help the most fragile members of the community, since the next verse speaks of pursuing peace and holiness.

For today: think of someone in your church or family who is walking weakly in faith. Take care with your example, with consistent choices and kind words, so that your way of living makes their path easier. Walk alongside them with prayer and patience, without judging them.
exp.8:21:
This verse says that, according to the law of Moses, almost everything was cleansed with blood. Without the shedding of blood, there was no forgiveness. "Forgiveness" here means the pardon of sins, and "cleansed" means made clean so that a person could draw near to God.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He reminds them how Moses used blood to confirm the covenant with Israel. His purpose is to show that all of that pointed to something better: the sacrifice of Christ, who entered heaven itself on our behalf.

For today: we do not have to earn forgiveness through effort or guilt. Christ has already given his life for us. When you feel the weight of a wrong, come to God with confidence and gratitude, knowing that forgiveness has already been paid for.
exp.10:27:
He says that Moses, by faith, kept the Passover and commanded that the blood of the lamb be sprinkled. The sprinkling of the blood refers to that blood placed on the doorposts. "He that destroyed the firstborn" is the destroyer sent in the last plague on Egypt. Because of that sign, the firstborn of Israel were not touched.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, encourages believers who were under pressure and temptation to turn back. He gives them examples of faith, and here shows Moses trusting in God's word, even though he did not yet see the result. After the Passover come the crossing of the sea and the fall of Jericho. Many Christians see in the lamb's blood a picture of Christ.

Today, faith is not only feeling confident but obeying what God says. Think of a step of obedience you have put off, and take it today, trusting in his promise.
exp.2:17:
To whom did God swear that they would not enter into his rest? The answer is: to those who did not obey. "Swore" means that God made a solemn promise, in this case a serious warning. The word "to" in the verse is the same word the explanation was pointing to, so the comment about an old spelling is removed. The "rest" was the promised land, where the people would find relief from their journey through the wilderness.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to give up. He reminds them of what happened to Israel after leaving Egypt. Many heard God, but they hardened their hearts. The following verse explains that they did not enter because of unbelief: the lack of trust showed itself in disobedience.

For today: true faith trusts God and shows itself in obeying him. Today, if God speaks to you through his Word, do not harden your heart; take a concrete step of obedience.
exp.10:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel crossed the Red Sea as if it were dry land, and they did it by faith. When the Egyptians tried to do the same, the sea covered them and they were drowned.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, reviews heroes of faith to encourage believers who were facing pressure and suffering. Here he reminds his readers that Israel, just freed from Egypt, trusted God before the sea and the army that was pursuing them. The story is found in Exodus 14.

For today: when you lack a clear path ahead, take the step God shows you, even if you cannot see the whole way. Faith does not wait until everything is clear; it trusts that God knows how to open a way where we see only an obstacle.
exp.4:3:
No one takes this honor on himself. That position of high priest is received only from the one whom God calls, as happened with Aaron. Here "honor" means an office of dignity and service before God, not simple praise.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) explains what a high priest was: a weak man, able to understand those who had gone astray, who offered sacrifices also for his own sins. Then he shows that Christ fulfills this: he did not appoint himself, but the Father called him. In this way the theme of Jesus as the eternal priest is prepared.

For today: do not seek positions or recognition out of ambition. Ask God what he is calling you to, serve with humility, and trust that he opens doors in his own time.
exp.5:2:
It says that the author and his readers are going to move on toward maturity in faith, and that they will do so "if God permit," that is, if God wills it. The word "perfection" here points to maturity, not to being without sin.

The author of Hebrews (we do not know for certain who he was) writes to believers who had grown stagnant. He encourages them to stop repeating the basics, such as repentance and faith, and to grow in the knowledge of Christ. With this phrase he acknowledges that everything depends on God. He then gives a serious warning about those who turn away, a passage that Christians interpret in various ways.

For today: make plans to grow spiritually, such as reading the Bible regularly and serving others, but with humility, depending on God and saying, "If God wills."
exp.3:6:
It says that God again marked out a special day, the "today," and that he did so a long time later, speaking through David. "Determines" means that God fixes or marks a time. "If ye will hear" means the same as "if you hear," and "harden not" means "do not be stubborn." The invitation is to listen to God with an open heart.

The author of Hebrews writes to Jewish believers and quotes Psalm 95, which David wrote centuries after the people of Israel failed in the wilderness. His argument is that if God was still saying "today" in David's time, the promise of rest had not run out. There was still an opportunity to enter it.

For today: do not put off what God is showing you. When you sense that He is speaking to you through His Word, respond today with humility and obedience, before your heart gets used to saying "no."
exp.6:9:
This verse says that Levi, the ancestor of the Jewish priests, had not yet been born when Abraham met Melchizedek. For this reason the expression "in the loins of his father" is used, which is an old way of saying that Levi was, in a certain sense, within his ancestor, as part of his future descendants.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named and whose identity is uncertain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus, a priest "after the order of Melchizedek," is greater than the Levitical priesthood. If Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek, then the descendants of Levi gave one too, and so Melchizedek is greater. It is an argument in the style of his time.

For today: we do not need another mediator to draw near to God. Jesus is our perfect and permanent priest. Today you can pray with confidence, without fear, because He represents you before the Father.
exp.10:33:
By faith, the heroes of God's people experienced great deliverances. They quenched the violence of fire, meaning they put out flames that were extremely strong. They escaped the edge of the sword, that is, they got away from the sword. "Waxed valiant" means they grew strong and brave. They were made strong out of weakness, and they turned to flight the armies of the enemy, which means they made enemy armies run away.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were tired and tempted to give up. He shows them examples from the Old Testament, such as Daniel and his friends, David, and others. He wants to encourage them to keep trusting God. Then he says that others suffered without being delivered, and they also remained faithful.

For today: trust God both when he delivers you and when he asks you to endure. His faithfulness does not depend on the outcome you hope for, and he cares for you in both cases.
exp.7:9:
It says that God will make a new covenant with Israel. The word "establish" means to set something in place or arrange it firmly. Instead of laws written only on stone, God will put them in the mind and write them on the heart. In this way there will be a close relationship: He will be their God, and they will be his people.

The author of Hebrews quotes here the promise from Jeremiah 31:31-34. He writes to Christians of Jewish background to show that Jesus is the mediator of a better covenant. The earlier context recalls that the covenant at Sinai was broken because of the people's unfaithfulness. Christians understand that this new covenant is fulfilled in Christ, although some debate how it relates to the future of Israel.

For today: obedience to God does not come from outside pressure, but from a heart that He transforms. Ask Him that you not only know His Word, but love it and live it from the inside.
exp.0:4:
This verse asks a question: to which of the angels did God ever say, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you"? And also: "I will be his Father, and he will be my Son." The word "begotten" here speaks of a unique relationship of Father and Son. The implied answer is: to none of them.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus is superior to the angels, who were held in great honor. He quotes Psalm 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14. The angels are servants of God; only Jesus is called Son in this full sense.

For today: you do not need intermediaries to draw near to God. Jesus, the Son, has already made the purification for your sins. Pray with confidence, and let his place of honor give you security.
exp.2:2:
This verse says that Jesus deserves more honor than Moses, just as the builder of a house deserves more honor than the house itself. "Glory" here means honor, and "dignity" means worth or respect. "Built" is an older word for constructed. Moses was highly respected, but Christ holds a higher place.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and whom people have debated much, writes to Jewish believers who valued Moses greatly. He wants to encourage them not to turn back, showing them that Jesus is superior. The verses that follow say that God is the one who created everything, and that Moses was faithful as a servant.

Today we can ask ourselves: does Jesus hold first place in my life? We can admire good leaders and teachers, but only Christ deserves our deepest trust and worship.
exp.8:19:
This verse records the words of Moses when he sealed the covenant at Sinai. "Testament" here means "covenant," a solemn agreement. The blood showed that this covenant was serious and came from God. "Has commanded you" means that God had ordered it.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers of Jewish background and recalls what happened in Exodus 24. Moses read the law to the people and sprinkled them with blood. He wants to show that even the first covenant did not begin without blood, and so he prepares the idea that the new covenant is sealed with the blood of Christ.

For today: God does not treat his covenant lightly. Today you can come to him with gratitude, knowing that Christ paid a very high price for you. That gratitude can lead you to obey him with joy and to take your commitments to him seriously.
exp.0:8:
He says the Son loved what is right and hated what is wrong. Therefore God, who is his God, anointed him (chose him and honored him) with the oil of gladness, that is, with joy and honor, above his companions. That word can refer to other kings or to those who share his kingdom with him; interpreters understand it in different ways.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, quotes Psalm 45:6-7. He wants to show that Jesus is greater than the angels. God calls the angels servants, but he calls the Son God and gives him an eternal throne. His reign is just because he loves righteousness.

For today: ask God that your heart may love what is good and reject what is evil, as Jesus did. Today, choose one small decision where you can act with honesty, even if it costs you. That is where a life of true joy begins.
exp.6:3:
Consider how great Melchizedek was, to whom even Abraham, the patriarch and father of the people of Israel, gave a tenth of the best of the spoils of war.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to return to their former faith. He wants to show that Jesus is superior to the priesthood of Levi. He uses Melchizedek, who blessed Abraham, to point out that this priesthood is earlier and greater, and that it points to Christ.

For today: Jesús is greater than any tradition or religious figure we might trust in. Today we can give him first place, and give with gratitude, recognizing that everything we have comes from God.
exp.4:13:
The explanation says that solid food is for the mature, meaning those who, through constant practice, have trained their spiritual senses to tell good from evil. "Strong meat" here means food for full-grown people, people complete in their development. "Use" refers to continual use, to practice.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, lovingly rebukes believers who had already been in the faith for some time, yet still needed the basics, the milk. They ought to have been teachers, and yet they were stuck. He speaks to them this way to encourage them to grow.

For today: maturity does not come on its own with the years, but through practice. Read the Bible regularly and apply what you learn to concrete decisions. In this way your judgment is sharpened little by little, and you will be better able to discern what pleases God.
exp.2:10:
God, angry at the rebellion of his people, made a solemn oath: that generation would not enter his "rest." The word "sware" means that he promised something with complete seriousness. "Rest" means peace, security, and quiet trust in God's presence.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 95, in which the Holy Spirit speaks and presents the words of God. He reminds us of the people of Israel in the desert, who doubted God and tested him for forty years, even while they saw his works.
