Because of their unbelief, that generation did not enter the promised land. The writer uses this as a warning for the believers of his own time. Interpreters explain in various ways how serious the warning is, but all agree that it calls us to persevere in faith.

Today, do not harden your heart. When God speaks to you through his Word, respond with trust and obedience, and seek the encouragement of other believers every day.
exp.9:36:
It says that there is only a very little time left before the One who was promised arrives, and that when he comes he will not delay. "Yet a little while" means "within a very short time." "Will come" refers to the Messiah, that is, to Christ, who is returning.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers who were tired, who had endured mockery and losses for following Jesus (Hebrews 10:32-34). He wants to encourage them not to give up. He quotes the book of Habakkuk, and no one knows for certain who wrote Hebrews. The phrase "will not tarry" is understood from God's perspective, for whom time is not measured as it is for us.

For today: when the waiting feels long and you grow weary of doing good, remember that God keeps what he promises. Keep trusting him, pray, and remain faithful today, even if you do not yet see the result.
exp.5:7:
It says that a land which, after receiving the rain, produces only thorns and briers (harmful, prickly plants) is of no use. The word "rejected" means turned away as worthless. It is close to being cursed, and its end is to be burned, the way a field overgrown with weeds is cleared.

The author of Hebrews was writing to believers who were at risk of turning away from Christ. He uses the image of the field: the same rain falls on the whole land, but the fruit shows the difference. Christians interpret this passage in various ways: some see a warning about losing salvation, others about a faith that was never genuine. Even so, the author quickly encourages his readers with hope.

Today it invites us to ask ourselves what fruit we are producing with everything God has given us. We can ask him to help us grow in love and faithfulness, and not to take his grace lightly.
exp.8:1:
This verse describes the first part of the tabernacle, the holy tent that Israel used in the wilderness. In it were the lampstand, the table, and the bread that was set out before God. This first space was called the Sanctuary, or the Holy Place.

The writer of Hebrews addresses believers of Jewish background and compares the first covenant with the new one. Before showing that Christ fulfills everything, he describes the tabernacle in detail. We do not know for certain who wrote the letter, but his purpose is clear: to show that Jesus is better than the ancient rites.

For today: the lamps, the table, and the bread point to light, fellowship, and provision. Today we can draw near to God through Christ, without complicated rituals. Take a moment today to pray with confidence, giving thanks that you have access to Him.
exp.4:8:
It says that Jesus, after being made perfect, that is, brought to his goal or completed in his work, became the source of eternal salvation for those who obey him. Here "salvation" means rescue from sin and its consequences, not only well-being of the body. Being made perfect does not mean that Jesus had any flaws, but that he completed the path the Father had given him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who are weary and full of doubts. He has just shown Jesus as the Son who suffered and learned obedience. Now he says that this path of suffering opened salvation for others, and he presents him as high priest in the manner of Melchizedek.

For today: obedience to Christ is not a burden to earn heaven, but the confident response to the One who already walked the hard road for us. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience, even if it costs you, trusting that he understands you.
exp.9:34:
This verse urges us not to let go of our confidence in God. The word "recompense" means a reward or prize, and "reward" reinforces the idea: that confidence has a great reward. Put simply: do not throw away your faith, because it is worth a great deal and God will reward it.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers who had already suffered mockery, imprisonment, and the loss of their possessions, and who had been sustained by the joy of hoping for something better. Now they may have been growing weary. He reminds them of their past courage to encourage them to remain steadfast until what was promised arrives.

Today, when you grow tired of waiting or of doing good without seeing results, remember how God sustained you before. Write down one time he helped you and return to that memory. Trust him for one more day.
exp.1:0:
It says that we ought to pay much closer attention and care to what we have heard, so that we do not gradually drift away. The phrase "it is necessary" means that this is required. "Let us pay attention" is the idea of giving careful heed. The image of "drifting away" is of something that slips or slides off without our noticing, like a boat carried off by the current.

The author of Hebrews does not identify himself; we do not know with certainty who he is. He writes to Christians of Jewish background, and he has just shown that Jesus is superior to the angels. That is why he says "therefore": since the Son is so great, his message deserves our full attention. The verses that follow warn that we must not neglect a salvation so great.

For today: we usually do not drift away all at once, but slowly, through carelessness. Set aside a fixed time each day to read the Bible and pray, and look for a community of believers who can help you stay firm.
exp.3:13:
It says that we have a great high priest, Jesus, the Son of God, who passed through the heavens and now stands in the presence of God. "High priest" here means one who brings the people together with God. "Confession" means what we declare we believe. For that reason, the text encourages us to remain firm in that faith.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who are weary and tempted to give up. He has just spoken of the Word of God that sees everything. Now he comforts them: Jesus is not a distant judge, and in the verses that follow it is said that he understands our weaknesses.

For today: when you feel weak or want to abandon your faith, do not rely only on your own strength. Pray with confidence to Jesus, who understands you, and stay firm one day at a time.
exp.6:19:
The explanation says that Jesus's priesthood was not established without God making an oath. The verse's words "inasmuch as" mean "because" or "since", and the phrase is left incomplete and finished in the next verse: the other priests were made without an oath, but Jesus was made with one.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is superior to the Levitical priesthood. He quotes Psalm 110:4, where God swears that his priest will be one forever. An oath from God shows that his decision is firm and definitive.

For today: you can rest in the fact that your relationship with God through Jesus does not depend on your strength or your steadiness, but on a firm promise that God upholds. When you doubt, remember that He committed Himself with an oath.
exp.9:7:
This verse repeats what the writer of Hebrews has just quoted from Psalm 40: God did not want, and took no delight in, the sacrifices and offerings. The word for "offering" means a gift presented to God, and "burnt offering" refers to a sacrifice that was burned up completely. The parenthesis clarifies that these were the things the law of Moses commanded to be offered.

The writer of Hebrews speaks to believers of Jewish background and explains that the ancient sacrifices could not remove sin at its root. He places the words of the psalm in the mouth of Christ, who announces that He would come to do the will of God. In this way he prepares the next step: the old gives way to the new.

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through religious effort. Rest in what Christ has already done, and respond with an obedience that comes from gratitude, not from fear.
exp.9:4:
This verse says that Christ, when he came into the world, spoke to God the Father. He said that God did not want sacrifices or offerings, but that God had prepared a body for him. The word "prepared" in the verse is the one used here for what God did.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 40:6-8 and places it on the lips of Jesus. He has just explained that the blood of animals cannot take away sins, and only reminds people of them each year. So God prepared another way: a human body for Christ, who would offer himself in obedience. It should be noted that Hebrews here follows the ancient Greek translation of the Psalm, which says "body," while the Hebrew text says something different ("you have opened my ears"). Scholars explain this in several ways.

God does not seek empty rituals, but obedient hearts. Today, instead of trusting in keeping religious duties, we can trust in what Christ did for us and respond to him with sincere obedience.
exp.9:29:
This verse reminds us that God is the one who carries out justice. The author quotes two phrases from the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:35-36): "Vengeance belongeth unto me" and "The Lord shall judge his people." Where the explanation speaks of the meaning of the quoted words, the justice that corrects wrong is the meaning of "recompense" in this verse, and the fair response of God to what each person has done is what "recompense" refers to.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to Jewish Christians who were tempted to abandon Christ because of pressure and suffering. He warns them that rejecting Jesus, after knowing the truth, is something very serious. God judges with justice, even his own people.

For today: when someone hurts you, do not take revenge; leave justice to God. At the same time, live with seriousness and gratitude the faith you received, without taking lightly what Christ did for you.
exp.9:28:
This verse asks a strong question: if someone who despised the law of Moses died without mercy, how much worse will the punishment be for the one who rejects Christ? To "trample underfoot" means to step on something and treat it with contempt. To "count the blood of the covenant an unholy thing" is to regard as common and worthless the blood of Jesus, which seals the new covenant. To "do despite to the Spirit of grace" is to insult the Spirit who offers forgiveness.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were tempted to turn back under pressure and suffering. He warns them that deliberately abandoning Christ is very serious. Interpreters debate whether he is speaking of true believers who lose their salvation or of those who only professed faith.

Today, let us not take lightly what Christ has done. Let us value his sacrifice with gratitude, and if we drift away, let us return to him with humility and not with indifference.
exp.5:13:
It says God promised Abraham, with an oath: "Surely I will bless you, and I will make your descendants very numerous." The phrase "blessing I will bless... multiplying I will multiply you" is a Hebrew expression that adds emphasis: it means that it will certainly happen.

The author of Hebrews speaks to Christians who were growing weary in their faith. He asks them not to be slow or discouraged, and to imitate those who waited patiently. He quotes the promise of Genesis 22:16-17 to show that God not only spoke but swore by himself. Abraham waited a long time, and the promise was fulfilled step by step.

For today: when you feel that God is taking a long time to answer, remember that his word is firm. You can keep trusting and waiting patiently, relying on what he has already promised in the Bible, even though you do not yet see the full result.
exp.0:12:
This verse asks a rhetorical question: to which of the angels did God ever say, "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet?" The answer is: to none of them. The place at the right hand stands for honor and authority. The footstool is the low seat where the feet rest; placing enemies under the feet speaks of complete victory.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, quotes Psalm 110:1. He wants to show believers of Jewish background that Jesus is superior to the angels. The angels serve, but only the Son is invited to reign with God.

For today: when you feel that evil is advancing or that your problems are too big, remember that Christ already reigns and his final victory is secured. You can rest and obey with hope, without fear.
exp.11:14:
We are told to look out for one another so that no one falls short of the grace of God, that is, his favor and help, which we do not deserve. It also warns that no "root of bitterness" should spring up: a resentment that takes hold, sprouts, and does damage. "Defiled" means stained or harmed. "Trouble you" means that it causes problems for you.

Context: the author of Hebrews, who is not named in the letter, writes to believers who are weary and pressed by hardships. He asks them to persevere, to seek peace, and to pursue holiness. The mention of a "root of bitterness" recalls Deuteronomy 29:18. Right after this, he gives the example of Esau, who despised what was precious for something momentary.

For today: if you hold a grudge against someone, do not let it grow. Bring it to God, ask his help to forgive, and, if possible, seek reconciliation before that bitterness affects you and others.
exp.10:31:
It says the author has so many examples of faith that there would not be enough time to tell about all of them. He names only a few: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets. The phrase about running out of time means he would not have enough time to speak about each one.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were under pressure and were tempted to give up. He has already reviewed the faith of Abraham, Moses, Jericho, and Rahab. Now he speeds up and names several people at once. Many of them were imperfect people, and yet Scripture remembers them for their trust in God.

For today: your faith does not have to be perfect to be real. God worked through weak and fallible people who trusted him. Today you can take a step of obedience, even if you have doubts, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that Christ did not enter the holy place with the blood of animals, as the ancient priests did, but with his own blood. He did it once for all, meaning in a definitive way, and so obtained eternal redemption. "Redemption" means rescue or deliverance. The "holy place" refers to the innermost sanctuary, where the blood was presented before God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Christ is superior to the priesthood and the sacrifices of the old covenant. Those rites were temporary, lasting until a time of setting things right, and they pointed toward something better.

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through repeated efforts. You can rest in what Christ has already done and draw near to God with confidence, thankful and ready to serve him.
exp.10:12:
This verse says that the heroes of faith mentioned earlier, such as Abraham and Sarah, died trusting God even though they did not see the promises fulfilled. They saw them from a distance, believed them, and welcomed them with joy from afar. They acknowledged that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth, travelers just passing through, because their true home was not in this land.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not reveal, writes to believers who were facing pressure and temptation to abandon their faith. He reminds them that others before them waited patiently. Although Sarah and Isaac did see a partial fulfillment, the complete promise still lay ahead.

For today: when a prayer or a dream takes a long time to come true, do not lose heart. Keep trusting God and live as someone who knows that their ultimate hope is in Him.
exp.5:3:
This verse begins a sentence that continues in the verses that follow. It says that those who were "enlightened" (who came to understand the truth of the gospel), tasted the heavenly gift and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and then fell away, cannot be brought back again to repentance. To "fall away" means that they turned away from the faith.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians tempted to abandon Christ. He has just spoken of moving on toward maturity. Christians have interpreted this passage in several ways: some see a real loss of salvation; others see a warning about a false faith or a total and final rejection of Christ.

Today, this text invites us to take our faith seriously. Let us not let it grow cold or abandon it under pressure. Let us cultivate prayer, the Word, and fellowship with other believers every day.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that Jesus had to become like us, his brothers and sisters, in every way. In this way he could be a compassionate and faithful high priest before God. The word "high priest" here refers to the chief priest, and "make reconciliation" means to cover or wipe away sin through a sacrifice.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that Jesus became human, a descendant of Abraham, to free us from the fear of death. Because he himself suffered and was tempted, he understands our struggles and can help us.

For today: when you feel alone, tired, or tempted, remember that Jesus truly understands you. Speak to him with confidence in prayer, without pretending or hiding, because he is compassionate and offers you forgiveness and help.
exp.12:7:
This verse says that Jesus Christ does not change: he is the same in the past, in the present, and in the future. "Forever" means "for all time." His character, his love, and his power remain firm.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were facing pressures. He reminds them of their former leaders, who taught them the faith and lived it. Those leaders were no longer there, but Christ remains. Because of this, the author then warns them against strange teachings that could lead them astray.

When everything around you changes, such as your work, your health, or the people in your life, you can lean on someone who does not change. Today, in prayer, hand over one worry and remember how Christ has been faithful before. His past faithfulness is a reason to trust him now.
exp.2:1:
It says that Jesus was faithful to God the Father, who appointed him to his mission, just as Moses was faithful in all of God's house. The people of God are what the "house" refers to.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who may have been tempted to give up or turn back. To encourage them, he compares Jesus with Moses, whom they greatly respected. He acknowledges Moses' faithfulness, but he prepares the way to show that Christ is superior.

Today we can learn that faithfulness matters to God. Jesus was faithful to the end, and that gives us confidence to follow him. We can ask him for help to be faithful in what he has entrusted to us, even if it seems small: our family, our work, or our service in the church.
exp.12:20:
It says that God, the God of peace mentioned in the previous verse, is the one who prepares and equips believers to do every good thing and to carry out his will. He himself works in them what pleases him, and he does this through Jesus Christ. For that reason, glory is given to Christ forever.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the letter does not mention (tradition has proposed several and there is no certainty), closes his message with a prayer of blessing. After urging his readers to persevere and to live faithfully, he now places his trust in God, not in human strength.

For today: when you want to do good but feel weak, ask God to equip you and to work in you. Obedience does not depend only on your own effort; God gives you what you need through Jesus.
exp.7:1:
He says that Jesus, our high priest, serves as a minister in the sanctuary in heaven, called "the true tabernacle." This place was not set up by any human being, but by the Lord himself. "High priest" means chief priest, "minister" is someone who serves, and "set up" means that he raised it or established it.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers of Jewish background who may have wanted to return to temple practices. He summarizes his argument for them: Jesus is seated beside God and serves in the heavenly sanctuary, which is superior to the earthly tabernacle. Scholars debate whether this sanctuary is a literal place or an image of God's presence, but the text emphasizes that its origin is divine.

Today, you can approach God with confidence, because Jesus intercedes for you in a place that no one can harm. You do not need to earn access through your own efforts.
exp.4:7:
He says that Jesus, although he was the Son of God, learned obedience through suffering. This does not mean that he had been disobedient before, but that he lived out obedience fully, even in pain. The word "consummated" (in the following verse) means "brought to its fullness" or "made perfect" in his mission.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who are tired and tempted to give up. He shows them that Jesus is the perfect priest because he understands human suffering. The previous verse recalls his anguished prayer, perhaps alluding to Gethsemane, though some interpret it more broadly.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not think that God is far away. Jesus knows that path. Ask him for help to obey him also in difficult moments, trusting that God can shape your character even through pain.
exp.10:10:
This verse says that Sarah, although she could not have children, received strength to become pregnant. She gave birth even though she was already past the age for it. The word "seed" means descendants, and the phrase "was delivered of a child" means that she gave birth. She was able to do this because she trusted that God would fulfill what he had promised.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who needed to persevere. He reviews examples of faith from the Old Testament. Earlier he spoke of Abraham, who lived as a foreigner while waiting for God's promise. Here he highlights Sarah, whose trust in a faithful God opened the way to a great number of descendants.

For today: when a situation seems impossible or far too late, remember that your trust rests on the faithfulness of God and not on your own strength. Today you can bring to him in prayer what you are hoping for, and choose to trust that he keeps what he promises.
exp.12:11:
It says Jesus died to make his people holy, that is, to set them apart for God and cleanse them, and he did this with his own blood. His suffering took place outside the gate, that is, outside the walls of Jerusalem. To be made holy means to be dedicated and made belonging to God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were pressured to return to their old rituals. He compares Jesus to the animals of the Day of Atonement, whose bodies were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16). Jesus was rejected and crucified outside the city, but there he accomplished something greater than those sacrifices.

For today: following Jesus may cost us approval or comfort. If you feel rejected for being faithful to him, remember that he went through this before, and that his blood has already made you his. Be encouraged to be faithful without being ashamed.

sum.10: Hebrews 11 explains that faith means trusting what God promises even when it cannot yet be seen, and that without faith it is impossible to please God. It recalls Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and many others, who trusted and obeyed even while suffering. All of them looked forward to something better, and God had prepared something better for us as well.
sum.5: The author encourages believers to move on toward maturity and seriously warns about those who receive great blessings and then turn away. He is confident that his readers will bear better fruit, and he asks them to persevere in faith and patience, as Abraham did. God's promise, affirmed with an oath, is a firm anchor for the soul, and Jesus has already entered on our behalf.
sum.7: Hebrews 8 teaches that Jesus is our High Priest, seated at the right hand of God and serving in the true sanctuary in heaven. His ministry is better because he is the mediator of a new covenant with better promises. Under it, God writes his law on the heart, everyone knows him, and he forgives sins forever.
sum.3: Hebrews 4 warns us that the promise of entering God's rest still stands, but we must receive it with faith and obedience, so that we do not fall short the way those did who refused to obey. God's word is living and powerful, cutting deeper than any sword, and it sees everything in our hearts. Jesus, our great High Priest, understands our weaknesses, so we can approach his throne of grace with confidence.
sum.11: Hebrews 12 encourages us to run the race of faith with patience, keeping our eyes fixed on Jesus, who endured the cross. God corrects us as a loving Father would, so that we may produce the fruit of righteousness, and He calls us to pursue peace and holiness. We have come to Mount Zion, so we should serve God with reverence.
sum.12: Hebrews 13 calls believers to live out their faith in everyday life: to love one another as brothers and sisters, to be welcoming to strangers, to remember those in prison, to honor marriage, and to be content without greed, because God will never abandon them. It asks them to follow Jesus, who does not change, and to obey their leaders. It ends with a blessing, asking that God would equip them to do his will.
sum.8: Hebrews 9 describes the tabernacle of the first covenant and the sacrifices that were repeated year after year, yet could not cleanse the conscience. Christ entered once and for all into heaven itself with his own blood and obtained eternal redemption. One day he will return, without sin, to save those who are waiting for him.
sum.2: Hebrews 3 invites us to fix our eyes on Jesus, who is faithful and greater than Moses. Moses was a servant in God's house, but Christ is the Son who is over it. It recalls how the Israelites, because of their unbelief and disobedience in the wilderness, did not enter God's rest, and so it encourages us not to harden our hearts, but to encourage one another every day and remain steadfast.
sum.9: Hebrews 10 teaches that the sacrifices under the law could not take away sin, but Jesus Christ, with one offering of his body, cleansed us and made us holy forever. Because of this, we can approach God with confidence, hold firmly to our faith, encourage one another, and not give up meeting with the congregation. The text warns against rejecting Christ and calls for steadfast endurance with patience.
sum.4: Hebrews 5 explains that every high priest is chosen from among men and is weak like them, and he does not give himself this honor but is called by God. Christ was called by God, learned obedience through suffering, and became the source of eternal salvation for those who obey him. The author rebukes his readers because they still act like children who need milk and must grow up.
sum.6: Hebrews 7 explains that Melchizedek, king of righteousness and of peace, blessed Abraham and received his tithes, which shows that his priesthood is greater than that of Levi. Jesus, from the tribe of Judah, is a priest forever according to that order, with God's oath. He lives always to intercede, and he offered himself once for all, so he brings us near to God and saves completely.
sum.1: Hebrews 2 calls us to pay close attention to the great salvation that God confirmed with signs and miracles. Jesus became human, made a little lower than the angels, and suffered death for everyone. In this way he defeated the power of the devil, freed people from the fear of death, and is able to help those who are being tempted.
sum.0: God spoke long ago through the prophets, but now he has spoken to us through his Son. He made the Son heir of all things and created the universe through him. The Son reflects God's glory, sustains all things, has cleansed our sins, and sits at the right hand of God. For this reason he is greater than the angels, who are servants sent to help those who will inherit salvation.
